subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, February 13, consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-38, an Act respecting the reorganization and divestiture of Teleglobe Canada, be now read the second time and referred to a legislative committee, and the amendment of Ms. McDonald (p. 3435).

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again I draw to the attention of Hon. Members the usual delaying amendment put forward by members of the New Democratic Party. I would have thought that the New Democratic Party would have gotten its act together sooner and realized that these delaying techniques of motion after motion really do not accomplish anything in the democratic process.
The Bill before us represents the difference in philosophy between the Progressive Conservative Party and the philosophy of the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party. It is our
Teleglobe Canada
belief that individuals, in their self interest and the combination of individuals working together in their self interest, will do the most good collectively for the development of all people and the development of our nation. It is the belief of members of the Opposition that the state, representing the citizens, is best able to look after the citizens. We have seen how that works in this country and in others. It is clear that the statism advocated by the New Democratic Party, in particular, and sometimes by the Liberal Party, does not work to create the efficiencies required by a nation.
We believe in market competition. We believe that the market creates the most efficient allocation of the resources of the country.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: Why are you creating a monopoly here, then?

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
The Member opposite and members of his Party believe in the state. They believe that the state should look after issues. They believe the state can best control things. They believe that the state, through the bureaucrats in the state, can best direct how the efficiency of the market-place or other efficiencies should be directed. We believe that the market-place, represented by entrepreneurship, giving individuals the opportunity to do what they as individuals want to do, and risking their money, creates the greatest advances in science, technology, manufacturing, distribution and trade. That advance is best for us all.
Members opposite believe that we are somehow in a static society and that the pie will never get any bigger. Members opposite believe that the state is the best apparatus of society to divide the pie more equally. Of course, what happens is that the pie becomes smaller and smaller.
We are now considering the Teleglobe Bill. The Opposition says, "Teleglobe is making all kinds of money, why don't you keep it?" They fail to realize that Teleglobe may be making money today, but it requires the continual injections of new entrepreneurial spirit, new technology, and new investment in order to make it grow and be competitive. If Teleglobe stopped growing and doing new things today, in five years Teleglobe would not make any money and it would be out of business. To a large extent, it depends on its cable. How long will cable for the transmission of messages be valued? When will cable cease to be the method of moving communication? Teleglobe has many new things that it must do. It must be entrepreneurial, and venturesome. There is one thing that the state is not, it is not venturesome. What we have to do today is make sure that Teleglobe is a successful company, and is given the opportunity to take advantage of the new technologies, the new outlooks, and the new ways of handling its mandate.
We believe that that can best be done by individual ownership. That is why in this Bill we have made sure that the employees of Teleglobe can buy into the company at a discount. I do not understand the Opposition's mentality when it says that this part of the Bill is wrong. We believe that if

February 16, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
individuals own the work within the scope of society, they will have an interest in making sure that we have a free society, because they will have something to protect. When the state owns all of the goods, services, property, and companies then there is nothing for the individual to protect because it is not his. Therefore, we say that this Bill is a watershed type Bill between state ownership and individual ownership.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: You know that you exaggerate.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: We believe it is important to cut down the size of Government, and we have been successful in cutting down its size. Every time we are able to get the Government out of an activity, we say that the Government is better off. We say that we as Canadians are better off to have these activities in the hands of individuals.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: Getting out of pensions, getting out of medicare, is that what you want to do? Is that the type of policy that you have? Get Government out of helping people, and get equality in this country.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: My friend says get Government out of helping people, as if Government was important. Does the Hon. Member not realize that people help people? You cannot see Government except in its bureaucracy, its big buildings, its regulations, and its red tape. That is the type of state that they want.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: The Hon. Member favours an end to medicare, an end to pensions. He does not think that we should support post-secondary education.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: Be quiet, Cassidy.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: Order, please. There will be an opportunity for Members' questions and comments, after the Hon. Member finishes his speech.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
I really do not mind them heckling me, because they know that we are saying some things that are true. They know that we are cutting them to the bone. They are the new dinosaur party. They believe in big Government, big state enterprises, and the collective, not individual freedom, democracy, private ownership, and freedom of the individual.
Since we have taken office we have accomplished a number of things. We have completed the sale of the Northern Transportation Company Ltd. To a large extent, we have sold and disposed of 23 million shares of Canada Development Corporation. I point out that we sold those for $11.50 a share. The market does not believe that they are worth $11.50 a share at this point, but that was a very worthwhile sale for the people of Canada. We have disposed of Canadian Arsenals Ltd. We have sold the CN Route, which was a losing trucking enterprise, to individuals who think that they can make money at trucking. That will keep more people employed, and it will move goods more cheaply. We have sold Pecheries Canada
Inc., a co-operative, for $5 million, subject to some adjustments. We have sold Canadair to Bombardier. We have sold our interest in Nanisivik Mines Ltd. In this Bill we have sold Teleglobe Canada.
Our aim and objective is to get the Government out of the business field to the greatest possible extent. The Government cannot work in business; it has too many conflicting objectives. When it goes into a commercial enterprise it has the objective of trying to make a dollar. On the other hand, its other objective is to try to make sure that some particular social good is accomplished. When a board of directors has those two conflicting mandates, usually what happens is the corporation does not operate as profitably and as aggressively as it might. Our belief is that if we can get Government out of the issue and, on a tender basis, buy from the private market-place those things that are necessary for the development of the social causes and problems of the country, we will accomplish a great deal more than having the state own enterprises involved.
I wish to address this particular deal for a moment. Some people have said that this is a deal where the minnow swallows the whale. In this case we have a situation where a relatively small company is taking over this company called Teleglobe. It is taking over Teleglobe with some pretty impressive backers. It has the backing of the National Bank, some very successful venture capital companies, the backing of the Caisse de Depot et Placement du Quebec, and the backing of competent management.
The offer that was made and was examined independently by Dominion Securities, and by a very capable board in the Canada Development Investment Corporation. That board came to the conclusion that the offer by Memotec that we are considering today is an offer that is a good for Canada.
It is a good offer on a number of grounds. First, the price is a pretty fair price. We could have received more for the asset if we had given it to a consortium of the telephone companies in order that they could have preserved their monopoly. We could have given it to CN-CP and they could have put it together and controlled overseas communication. We could have forgotten about the Competition Act, and about the fact that we need new, aggressive action in technology development. Perhaps we could have received more money that way. The fact is that this was the best offer that falls within the concepts of the Competition Act and it is to an independent, separate, new company that, on a new basis, can handle this sale. It is a good transaction as opposed to one that is transferring the activity over to another regulated body, and extending a monopoly position.
Second, the transaction contemplates some competition in the field of transmission. It certainly contemplates that if the licence is to continue, there will have to be a 13.5 per cent cut in overseas telephone rates and a 10 per cent cut in telex rates by 1988. It also contemplates that the charges which the company will be able to levy will have to be no more than 2 per cent above the average rate charged by Bell and BC Tel. There
February 16, 1987

is some real control on the prices the company can charge for its services.
Aside from that type of control, we must remember that we live in an age of increasing technology. Despite regulation, the company will have to be prepared to compete in that new technology. This is a small world, and it is getting smaller. Other countries in the world have satellites, and satellite communication is possible. No matter how hard we try, we are not able to prevent people from using that technology. The CRTC and some people involved in broadcasting would like to prevent people from using a dish to collect television signals. They have not been very successful in that regard. I suggest that they will not be successful as the technology becomes more readily available and more reasonable in cost.
Looking at the whole picture, despite the present monopolytype arrangement concerning transmission overseas by telephone companies and the like, the company will not be able to maintain that position forever. If the company's rates are not kept competitive, others will install and use communications systems which are more competitive.
The deal must be commended. The Government has been able to ensure that individual employees will be protected, particularly their pension rights. Often we see takeovers of companies where pension arrangements are somehow slithered by and the employees wind up with something very much different from what they had when they were working for their former employer.
Also from the point of view of the employee, this is a situation where in a sense a relatively small company is taking over a relatively large organization. If this were a situation where Bell Canada was taking over Teleglobe, it may well have been a situation where employees could be replaced, or there might be situations of efficiency which would cause the replacement of people. This is a situation where the employees are protected and looked after from a pension point of view and from a job point of view. As I mentioned earlier, even more important, they will be given the opportunity to become more personally involved with the right to buy up to 5 per cent of the stock at a 10 per cent discount.
The Bill should not be delayed. It should be expedited. Is there any reason to hold it up? Is there any real reason to say that the Government must be involved in owning telecommunications? Not at all. Let us get the country back on the free road. Let us get the Bill passed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I distinctly heard the Hon. Member, who is my colleague on the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, saying some things which I think most of his colleagues in the Conservative Party would repudiate. He was saying "the less government, the better; the less government intervenes in people's lives, the better". He became quite agitated when I suggested that he was advocating the Government get out of medicare, that the Government
Teleglobe Canada
get out of providing old age pensions for older Canadians, and that the Government, in fact, get out of being involved in a number of different social services which provide the basis for a humane and compassionate society.
I am really rather concerned. We have heard about the reemergence of a kind of Monday club among back-benchers in the Progressive Conservative caucus. Their feeling seems to be that there is great support out there among the public and that if only these views were to be put to the fore by the Government, somehow their standing in the opinion polls would rise from the current abysmal level of 23 per cent. Perhaps those are the Hon. Member's views. Perhaps he is suggesting or advocating the privatization of medical care insurance and hospital insurance, returning to the situation which exists in the United States where half the people who are homeless are in that situation because they were uninsured and were hit by heavy medical care expenses. This is the kind of dog-eat-dog society about which the Hon. Member seems to be talking.
I should like to ask him to be perhaps more precise and to repudiate those views which I do not think are the views of Canadians as a whole. I certainly hope they are not the views of the Progressive Conservative caucus, even those who subscribe to the punitive Monday club which is being reestablished.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, here he is again, the finance critic of the New Democratic Party. He knows he is wrong on the Teleglobe Bill, so he raises a great big ogre indicating the Progressive Conservative Party will somehow interfere with medicare. What absolute nonsense. We are dealing with a commercial corporation which is profiting or in the business of telecommunications, running a cable system across the Atlantic. Suddenly he says, "By gosh, if you do that, you are going to do medicare next". Let us get realistic.
We have a medical care insurance scheme to which the federal Government contributes. It is run on a provincial basis. It is universal and generally applicable. It works well. It has produced medical care and coverage in Canada at a per centage of cost in GNP at less than that of the United States. We would be foolish to change that.
Running the telex across the Atlantic is not a matter which really affects the life, health, or well-being of Canadians. To say that we cannot have those things because somehow they might interfere with medicare is to stretch the imagination far beyond all realism.

Let us get down to brass tacks and let me ask him a question to which he can respond very honestly and sincerely. There is an old conservative principle, is there not, that one should not repair something if it is working? Mr. Speaker, I am glad my friend raised this issue. I think it goes to the essence of the reason for the sale. While it is true that the company presently is earning a return based on an amount somewhere between 8 per cent and 10 per cent on the money, and while it is true that that is now a little less than our long term borrowing rate, it is also true that this company is exposed to the greatest change in technology that we are likely to see as the world develops. In our view it is, therefore, important that we have in charge of that technology the most adventuresome, the most aggressive people that we can get to be prepared to invest, take chances and do the things necessary to exploit the oncoming new technologies.
We could keep the company and continue to get, as my friend mentions, perhaps $50 million a year. That would not last very long unless there were some massive changes in the structure and organization of the company in the future. The way to handle a situation like this is to sell when the situation looks good, when the company is making a profit because that is when it will sell and sell for the best price. If we were to hang on and hang on, we might well wind up not having a company to sell. It is far better to sell a profitable company when all is going well.

Member explain to the House, Mr. Speaker, how this new company, which was established at a very high debt-with a very small company buying a company that had something over $100 million in cash, if the business reports are accurate-carrying the kind of debt load it now carries, will be in a better position to adapt to new technology than the existing company? subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words on this Bill. My interest was sparked a few moments ago when I heard the hon. gentleman across the way refer to the trans-Atlantic cable, that is the cable that runs across the Atlantic Ocean. This cable takes whatever message you feed into it across the Atlantic. When you pick up your telephone here in Ottawa and you want to call Newfoundland or Nova Scotia, the transmission is carried by Bell Telephone and into the provincial telephone networks across the country. But when you want to call across the Atlantic, the transmission not only goes by Bell Telephone and over the lines of the telephone companies as far as Newfoundland, it is taken over by another company altogether. What we are talking about here is the trans-Atlantic link. We are talking about that owner of the cable, of the transmission across the Atlantic, being passed from Government hands into the hands of the private sector. That is as I understand it.
I am trying to pick some sense out of all the gobbledegook that some members are talking about today concerning financial transactions, shares, profits and everything else. It all boils down to the fact that you have private enterprise taking over a cable that is a monopoly. There is no other transmission from Canada across the Atlantic that I know of. There is in the United States, of course. The hon. gentleman is talking about a telex. That is a hundred years ago.
I rise in the debate because Newfoundland is the key link here. All cables go from Newfoundland across the Atlantic. That is the importance of Newfoundland. When you are talking about the telegraph, that is not the telephone. A hundred years ago or so the telegraph went from Heart's Content, Newfoundland right across the Atlantic over to Great Britain-from Heart's Content next to Heart's Desire next to Heart's Delight, and then the next place to that was where I was born, a place called Green Harbour, Trinity Bay. What is important is that the cable starts from Newfoundland and goes right across the Atlantic. What we are talking about today is not the telegraph but the telephone lines that were put across the ocean. The telephone lines went right across the Atlantic in the year 1956, to my recollection. They came into Clarenville, Newfoundland, and went right across the Atlantic to connect up somewhere in Ireland. We know that the Coast Guard has a ship that does checks on the cable across the Atlantic throughout the year. To my recollection, there is one ship, the Sir Humphrey Gilbert, that does that cable check. It has some pretty sophisticated machinery on board including small minisubs to check that particular cable.
We are not talking about anything complex. Hon. Members love to make things complex. When she announces a sale, the Minister wants to complicate matters. She does not even mention what is actually being sold to the private sector.
Teleglobe Canada
I suppose it boils down to whether or not the Government has a philosophy that the private sector should actually control the only communications monopoly between Canada and the other side of the Atlantic. The Bill boils down to whether or not private enterprise should be able, whenever it wishes after five years, to jack up the rates and do whatever it wants. In the Bill there is a 13 per cent cut, or something like that, along with controlled management of the private sector for the next five years. After five years it is open for the private sector to do whatever it pleases. That is what it all boils down to after reading through all the financial speeches we have heard in the House concerning this Bill.
There is nothing strange about the Government's philosophy to sell Teleglobe, a very profitable outfit. It made $80 million or $85 million, give or take $10 million or $20 million last year. It made $110 million, give or take $10 million or $20 million two years ago. It made over $100 million this year, give or take $10 million or $20 million. The question is not only whether the Government should have sold Teleglobe to the private sector, but if the private sector should have control over the one link across the Atlantic. It also boils down to the sale price.
Let me first deal with the monopoly aspect of this matter. Should the Government have sold this company to the private sector and should the private sector be allowed to control the only link across the Atlantic? The Canadians I know best think it is unfortunate that the communications and telephone system in Canada is, to a very great degree, in the hands of monopolies in each province. When I receive a complaint from a lady who says, "I did not telephone London, England, but I have a bill here from Bell or from Newfoundland Telephone or New Brunswick Telephone or Maritime Tel. I did not make that phone call, but I am being charged for it", what am I supposed to do? The telephone company has a monopoly. It says, "You either pay up or we disconnect your telephone, and if we disconnect your telephone you cannot get one back unless you pay up", and that is for something the lady does not owe. It is her word against the word of the telephone company. That is the danger inherent in monopolies.
If a person had oil delivered to his house and said that he did not receive the particular amount of oil the oil company is charging him for, then he would have a choice. He could go to another oil company. With electricity and telephones, it is different. People do not have a choice.
As far as ordinary Canadians are concerned-and by that, I mean people who do not buy RRSPs-the unfortunate aspect of the monopoly of the telephone company is something to be frowned upon. It is sometimes disgraceful to see how the telephone companies in Canada treat people; it is disgusting. The telephone companies need a lesson in something, I do not know what, because what they say goes whether we like it or not.
I found it strange, and I still find it strange today-perhaps Members of the House can tell me why, because I never could figure out why-that when there was a challenge to the

Teleglobe Canada
monopoly of Bell Telephone, the Government refused the challenge. I am talking about CN-CP's application for longdistance charges. It was refused because in the United States, where competition was allowed, rates would eventually go up. There appeared to be some unity here in this House. The Bell Telephone unions said that we could not break the monopoly, because if we did Bell employees might lose their jobs. When I think about that poor lady who did not telephone London, England, day but got charged for such a call, I have to say that the monopoly should be broken or the telephone companies should behave themselves and smarten up.
There is a motion presently before the Chamber for a three-month hoist proposed by a member of the New Democratic Party. As I understand it, the motion would allow the securities people to investigate something that has to do with an increase in Memotec's share cost. At least that is what the mover of the motion put as the reason for moving the motion. As far as I could find out, Memotec's stocks appear to have increased dramatically. I suppose this is because of the prospect of its purchasing Teleglobe, this monopoly that goes across the ocean. I suppose any company's stock would increase if it were to take over Teleglobe. I also notice that Memotec is the owner of a company in the United States, or is it the other way around-I do not know which. It appears as if the company has just as many employees in the United States as it has in Canada. It certainly must be a growing outfit if it has that kind of control.
As far as the Bill is concerned, it boils down to whether or not the Government should have sold the company for $488 million when its profits were running to about $100 million a year. Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, if you were able to purchase a company for $488 million while the profits of the company ranged at around $100 million a year. That is quite a remarkable sales contract. That would be something at which one would really have to jump. This is the sort of thing the private sector wants. It can watch the money roll in. Millions upon millions of dollars of profits are guaranteed because the purchaser will get his money back in four and a half or five years anyway, and then the rest of it, those few hundred million dollars a year, is all gravy.
Why did the Government of Canada do this? There is a very good reason. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) wants to stand up in this House on Wednesday and announce to everyone that he has trimmed the deficit down to-notice I say "down to"-$32 billion. Not $32 million or $32,000 or $3,200, but $32 billion. Half a billion for this outfit brings it down to $32 billion. That from a Government that was going to decrease the deficit. We have had the highest deficits in Canadian history since that Government came to power. If you add up the national debt since Confederation who is responsible for over half? That Government over there.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-38 is an example of doctrine. It certainly is not an example of good business sense. I am going to uncap some of the arguments which have been put forward by the government side. It must be made clear right off the bat that we are dealing with a monopoly. Teleglobe is a monopoly and under the Tory's proposal it will continue to be a monopoly.
The key argument put forward by Members, such as the Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), is that it is better for a few people to own something than all Canadians. Last year's profit ran close to $100 million. Each of the 25 million Canadians benefited by only a couple of thousand dollars. No one will dispute that. However, the Member for Mississauga and the Government claim that it is better for a few hundred or a few thousand Canadians, who have enough money to buy stocks and participate in a transaction like this, to divvy up $50 million or $100 million among a much smaller and more select group.
That is a doctrinaire argument. It is an argument by the rich for the rich to get richer. It has nothing to do with the significant point that Teleglobe is a monopoly. It was set up, not only to provide cable service, as the Member for Gander- Twillingate (Mr. Baker) said, but to provide satellite communication for Canadians throughout the world. It had set rates.
Government Members are trying to paint the management and workers at Teleglobe as a group of faceless, semi-competent or perhaps incompetent bureaucrats who have no entrepreneurial spirit, do not understand business, do not know how to do anything, and are designed to fail. They say that is why the Government has to get rid of this Crown jewel, one of the most profitable of Canadian Crown corporations.
From time to time we must bare the face of some of the ideologues on the government side. As an example, last week on my way back from British Columbia I met a Tory Member in the airport. I asked whether he was taking the direct flight to Ottawa. He said no, that that was an Air Canada flight and that he only flies CP. I asked him what time he would arrive in Ottawa and learned that he was prepared to spend an extra three hours to get back to work in Ottawa in order to ensure that the money of the people of Canada was spent only in private enterprise.
February 16, 1987 ___________________________COMMONS
We must understand that there are a large number of what I would describe as ideologically nose-ringed reactionaries on the government side. This document is clearly doctrine. It is not good business. Let us look at some of the guts of it. Every document put out by the Government says that the Government will get $608.3 million. The fact is that the Government will not get $608.3 million. At most it will get about $345 million. That is a fire sale price. As my colleague, the Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), has said many times, this is "minnow-tec". In 1983, only four years ago, this little teeny company had 30 employees. That is only four years ago.
What is happening only too often in Canada is little teeny companies using extreme leverage in the market-place. They borrow from the National Bank, and from here and there. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South and others say that because of all this entrepreneurial talent which will suddenly be injected, all of this great self-interest going out and fighting for new technology, we will suddenly be in a better position to buy world leading edge technologies in terms of fibre optics and new satellite technologies and so on. Nothing could be further from the truth. That is why the Tories have given over to "Minnow-tec" in this deal another five years of monopoly. The Tories say they are against monopoly, that they want free enterprise in the market-place. What a lot of ballyhoo. The monopoly is being kept 100 per cent intact in terms of this operation.
Is "Minnow-tec" really going to go out there and garner all of these new technologies and bring us into the forefront and actually benefit individual consumers? Nothing could be further from the truth. Its debt load alone means it is going to have to try to get more out of the consumer and less from technology. I think Members of the Government should be more cautious.
I have watched these kinds of deals coming from the ideologues on the right for some time. In my own Province of British Columbia, the former Premier, Bill Bennett, announced he was selling off the entire B.C. ferry fleet because it will be good for British Columbia. He sold it to a private group and leased it back on a five-year basis. We constructed the fleet, we bought and paid for it. Now we are in our second rollover, wherein every five years we buy the fleet back again through this leasing. That is an another example of these brilliant minds, these great business people the Tories hold themselves up to be. Nothing could be further from the truth. The consumers and real owners of those ferries get dinged time and time again, so this little group of free enterprisers, these great free enterprises, can sit at home and put their feet up. They have homes in Miami, Mexico, Europe and the Far East. They have big cabin cruisers, Cadillacs and so on. They are the smart ones who profit from these private deals, and that is what they are.
Almost no one in my constituency buys stocks or RRSPs. Unemployment in my constituency is close to 40 per cent.
DEBATES ____________________________________________3455
Teleglobe Canada
Members of the Government do not want to talk about that. But where is the Government planning to go? Is it planning to privatize the RCMP, for example, or sell Parliament Hill and lease it back to try to bring down the deficit? Is it planning to sell CN or Air Canada? Where is the Government planning to go? These are the kinds of things which are so important to look at in this debate.
I would like to deal for a moment with the important point made by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway, about a three-month hoist. There has been some jiggery-pokery in the market. That is pretty clear. Everyone has recognized that and an evaluation is being done. Is it proper for the House of Commons to pass into law a sale transaction when there has been jiggery-pokery in the market? What we are asking for is a hoist so we can look at that. I think it is only proper that the House of Commons, the representatives of the Canadian electorate have a chance to look at what actually went on behind the scenes in this transaction. No Member of the Government is saying, obviously, we should not look at the jiggery-pokery, but what they are refusing to do is deal honestly in this debate with what a bad deal this really is.
I can give another example of where Members of the Government try to use double-speak just a little too often. The big oil companies back in the 1970s price fixed. That was pretty clear. A major investigation took place, not just in western Canada but right across the country. The big oil companies fixed, in terms of billions of dollars, the price of oil and gas and home heating fuels purchased by Canadian consumers. Did the Liberals do anything about that? No. Did the Tories do anything about it? No.
It is vitally important that in various sectors there be government owned and operated systems such as Petro-Canada, not just to have a window on the field but to have a hands-on experience with what is really going on so that the consumers can be protected.
I would like to take a look for a few moments at the guts of Teleglobe and what it really means to Canadians. In recent years, 85 per cent of its revenues have come from overseas telephone calls. I think we should look at what kind of money Teleglobe has been making. The Government turned it over for $345 million when it made close to $100 million in profit last year. Teleglobe has been around since 1949. By 1975 it was making over $10 million a year in profit. By 1982, five years ago, its profits were up to almost $50 million. Now it is skating close to $100 million.
What does it do? It handles all overseas telecommunications entering and leaving Canada. That includes telephone, telegraph, cable and Telex communications. Teleglobe is a joint owner of submarine ocean cables and telecommunication satellite systems. In 1985 Teleglobe's revenues totalled $678 million. In the same year, 1985, the total revenues of "Minnow-tec" were $17 million. Memotec began in 1983 with just 30 employees. I have nothing against Memotec. However, when the Hon. Member for Mississauga South and others talk

February 16, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
about this new infusion of entrepreneurial spirit from a little teeny company and try to paint Teleglobe as being some sort of dozy bunch of dinosaurs who could not possibly figure their way out of their own office space, it is a totally inaccurate and unfair representation. I think Members of the Government would be wise, when talking about Crown corporations and public servants, to remember that some of the people who are working in the public service, if not most of them, are very dedicated and often work for far less than many of their counterparts do in the private sector.
I think I have dealt effectively with the debunking of the ongoing blather from the Government's side that somehow $600 million is coming in. That is simply not the fact. Less than half that amount is coming in. Members of the Government say we need to get these hundreds of millions of dollars in to take down the deficit. From a straight business perspective, nothing could be further from the truth. Bringing in $300 million in one shot to apply against the deficit is nowhere near as beneficial, in bringing down the deficit, as it would be to keep Teleglobe and have that $100 million year after year going into the general revenues of the Government of Canada to use for other worthwhile purposes.
There are a number of reasons why all Canadians should oppose the Teleglobe sale; first, it has been a consistent moneymaker and, second, it is a monopoly, and a monopoly for good reason. Let me deal for a moment with the press release of the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) because it makes some preposterous points. For example, the news release states:
Teleglobe Canada will benefit by being able to pursue new business opportunities under skilled private sector management.
It does not bother to add that there will be five further years of absolute and total monopoly. A question which has to be asked when the Government points at Teleglobe and say, "We need new entrepreneurial spirit", is what has gone on for the last two and a half years? The Tories have been sitting opposite for two and a half years and they cannot keep pointing at the Liberals or New Democrats or someone else. The fact is that if there were areas in which efficiency could have been improved, the Government should have dealt with it.
The release goes on to state:
Consumers will benefit from an average rate reduction on overseas telephone calls exceeding 13 per cent in 1988. Of further importance, consumer interests will be protected into the future by CRTC regulation-a protection not currently present under crown ownership.
I suppose it is a fair statement for the Minister to make, but it is totally erroneous and unrelated to the situation. Teleglobe is completely managed by the Government of Canada, or it was until this point in time. For the Minister to say one of the key reasons for selling it off to the private sector is so it can come under some kind of consumer protection, is tantamount to fraud. Ministers should not go around cooking up reasons that have no foundation whatsoever in fact.
I would now like to return to the purchase price. A monopoly is being sold off. Because it occupies the field of communications, in which there is a legitimate public policy interest to be protected, it should continue to be in the public realm owned by the Canadian public.
With respect to share ownership restrictions, the Government continues to crow about the good price that it received. Of course, it said existing domestic telephone companies could not buy into it because they were monopolies. It is good that it is a monopoly now. Members of the Government like the fact that it is staying a monopoly so that it can set whatever kind of price trends and so on that it wants. However, members of the Government do not want the other monopolies in on it. This is the point at which I say this whole debate comes from a doctrinaire position of the Government. It does not come from a position of good business. I think the Hon. Member for Mississauga South would be the first to admit that. This is not good business, whether we are talking about the national debt, how the money will be applied or even about the future leverage of "Minnow-tec" in the future in terms of buying new technologies.
The Government places the following requirements on the deal. Non-resident companies will be restricted to acquiring 20 per cent ownership of Teleglobe. They are not allowed ever to exert control. Foreign telecommunication companies are permanently barred from ownership of the company, and domestic companies can obtain up to 40 per cent in the near future, but ultimately that can never go above 33.3 per cent. Members of the Government make a big deal about the employees being eligible to purchase 5 per cent of the shares. I hope that a few Conservative Members have heard of things such as co-ops. Five per cent ownership at a 10 per cent discount is not a big deal in my view.
With respect to international obligations, there is something Members of the House should be taking a closer look at. I refer to what is happening in the United States. The U.S., in its so-called striving for more communication and more competition in telecommunications, has decided to renege on its commitment to INTELSAT. INTELSAT is dealt with in Clause 8 of the Bill. Both INMARSAT, which is the International Maritime Satellite Organization, and INTELSAT, which is the International Telecommunications Satellite Organization, were set up to try to assist some of the less developed countries of the world to obtain some type of crosssubsidization in telecommunications. A fixed rate was set under this international agreement whereby the same base rate that is applied in those areas of heavy traffic would be applied to areas of lower traffic, such as in most of the developing world. As the U.S. is backing out of this agreement and starting to put up its own satellites we see this "Minnow-tec" deal coming along. What will it mean? It may well mean that before too long-certainly before the end of its five-year monopoly-"Minnow-tec" will find itself in a conflict of interest situation. How will it deal in the most effective
February 16, 1987

manner for its shareholders, which is its primary role, to ensure that its shareholders are receiving the best type of return from the operation versus that of INTELSAT? The agreement that is set up to benefit other parts of the world is a very good idea in terms of communications in a world so often fraught with all types of violence and confrontations. It ensures that wherever possible there is reasonably good and accessible communications.
Down the road where will our domestic telephone companies go? Will they start buying out part of the link to the U.S. satellite system and get out of INTELSAT? What will that mean to a highly-leveraged operation such as Teleglobe? These are questions the Government does not seem to have addressed itself to, certainly not in debate thus far in the House of Commons.
Let us take a look at what other industrialized countries have done, those which have continued to participate in the international agreement and in the field of overseas communications. Australia, New Zealand, France, West Germany, Italy, Norway and Sweden all have totally government-controlled systems just like Teleglobe. They are not planning to make any changes. The U.K., from which the Government adopted this idea, made a share offering and privatized British Telecom but retained just below 50 per cent ownership. The British Government maintained a 49.9 per cent controlling interest in international telecommunications. The only two main players which are outside of all this are, of course, Japan and the United States, which have both gone to their own privately-controlled telecommunications systems.
There are inherent contradictions in selling a company that is a monopoly and keeping it as a monopoly. The arguments that have been put forward by the Government for not allowing the domestic telephone companies to buy into this company fall by the way when one takes a close look at the deal. Denying monopolies the right to buy a monopoly, thus allowing a small group to set up and maintain a monopoly, is a specious argument. Any Canadian who takes a look at this deal will see that this lucrative world-class Crown corporation was sold for a song. It was sold at far below what anyone would consider to be a reasonable price for such a valuable operation.
I see that I am running out of time and will therefore conclude my remarks. The Government is attempting to paint this sale as the sale of a Crown corporation that does not really need to be publicly owned in order to obtain some money to buy down the deficit. The argument is that private enterprise will be able to run it better. As I have pointed out, because of its highly debt-laden position "Minnow-tec" is not in as good a position to be buying into leading-edge technologies. In terms of protecting Canadian consumers that, again, is unlikely since the monopoly continues. The likelihood of rates coming down when a company with such a huge debt load has purchased a particular Crown corporation is unlikely to occur. I do not see any benefits to Canada's deficit, to the country, to the workers,
Teleglobe Canada
to consumers or to Canada's international obligations in terms of setting rates around the world.
I conclude by saying that practical wisdom denies this as being a good route to go. Bill C-38 has to be seen as a type of defective doctrine which I think will get the Government into a great deal more trouble.

Mr. Speaker, the speech by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) is typical of the kind of speeches he tends to make, full of exaggerations, and in this case, all Government-owned corporations are perfect and any company that has the misfortune to be a private corporation is rejected out of hand. Mr. Speaker, he contemptuously tells us that nobody in his riding owns shares. I think he ought to visit a few co-operatives, these people are shareholders. It is co-ownership, and there is nothing criminal about being a company co-owner. There must be many of them in his riding. It is rather unfortunate that he would choose not to speak for his constituents who happen to own their business.
I have a question for him. He tells us that a Crown corporation has everything going for it, that a profit-making Crown corporation ought to stay under public ownership. I might remind him about other Crown corporations which at first were operating in the red and which were bought by the Government precisely to set them back on a sound financial track-and Air Canada is a good example. They were to be resold to private interests because that was the purpose of the whole exercise, but they are still Crown corporations. Is Air Canada service better than CP Air's because it is a Crown corporation? A moment ago I asked the Hon. subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join in the debate today concerning the proposed reorganization and divestiture of Teleglobe Canada. As the Minister for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall) stated in her remarks, this is but the latest in a series of transactions, part of a process that is an integral part of our comprehensive approach to prudent government management, and one that is now moving into top gear.
When I sought nomination, one of the things that I found most discouraging about what was going on in the Government at that time was that the federal Government had an interest in about 400 private sector activities, not only Crown corporations. With the 400 interests there are 250,000 plus people who work for Crown corporations. I would suspect that many of these people are still working for Crown corporations today.
Others have or will be commenting on the benefits to Canadians which flow from this transaction. I wish to concentrate my remarks on the role of privatization in our economic agenda, and the need to continue this important management process. The privatization policy of this Government has been stated many times. Yet, despite the repetition, the opposition Parties have refused to listen, and they continue to follow their strategy of making privatization a matter of ideology.
In the 10 minutes remaining before the luncheon adjournment I should like to touch on some examples which have nothing to do with ideology but a lot to do with good common sense.
During the 1984 election campaign a poll was taken in Canada. Approximately 60 per cent or more Canadians indicated at that time that they did not want to see the federal Government become involved in more Crown corporations. They wanted to see the federal Government divest itself of those interests.
In October, 1986, not many months ago, there was an election in the Province of Saskatchewan. A CBC poll was taken at the time of 1,600 people in the province. Believe it or not, in the Province of Saskatchewan, with its long history of socialism, 76 per cent of them said that they had had their fill and did not want to see the Government involved in more Crown corporations.
The Saskatchewan Potash Corporation is a prime example to which socialists refer as their flagship. An Hon. Member from British Columbia just talked about Teleglobe being a Crown jewel. Other Members from the Province of Saskatchewan and myself can tell the House that investing literally hundreds of millions of dollars in the potash industry probably resulted in a rate of return to that province in the neighbourhood of 4 per cent or 5 per cent in good times, when in fact the money could have been earning a much higher rate of return for Saskatchewan taxpayers. The Saskatchewan Potash Corporation has turned out to be, not a flagship but a bit of a sinking ship at the moment. It is a very risky business. There
Teleglobe Canada
were days when money was made in that industry. However today, when prices are down and there is a lot of competition in the industry, we will probably lose $150 million because of that Crown corporation.
This is precisely why Governments, whether provincial or federal, should not become involved in Crown corporations. I say that it should be left to the business sector, to private enterprise. If they want to take the risks and reap the rewards, let them do so. We can take the royalties and the taxes.
I should like to refer to another example. On the late news on CTV on Saturday night I watched a clip from China showing an auction of Crown corporations. They were small businesses, but the point I want to make is an obvious one. China is a country which has had decades of socialism. Many of its Crown corporations have been locked up for three years. They were so inefficiently run that their doors were closed. Even China is starting to recognize that they should be sold to the private sector. Many young Chinese businessmen are interested in becoming involved in revitalizing the companies. As it turned out, there were higher bids than the Government expected. That is how eager the Chinese people were to become involved in these small businesses.
I should like to refer to another example. Recently I had the pleasure of visiting East Africa with the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade as part of our ODA review. As a student I had been to East Africa, 20-some years ago. I must say that it was disappointing to see what has happened to Tanzania over those years. Because of the socialistic experiment there, many sectors of its economy have in fact declined. I should like to refer to a story which appeared on the front page of a newspaper while we were there. It had nothing to do with our visit, but it had a lot to do with the restructuring of its Government and its economy. It was made very clear by the new leader of the country that they must divest themselves of some of their"parastatal" corporations, as they call them, because the management had been so poor and productivity had been so low.
Another example can be found in the United Kingdom where Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher has sold off shares in British Telecom and in British Gas. Just the other night there was talk of doing much the same with British Airways. If it were such a bad investment, why are so many people in Britain rushing out to buy shares? It has been a resounding success. The people of Britain recognize that it is a worthwhile venture in which to invest, and I would suggest that our divestiture of Teleglobe is along the same lines.
Socialists like to use two arguments when it comes to selling Crown corporations. First, if it is not successful, they like to say that the Government should hold on to it and protect the jobs. Can we imagine all the years the Government has held on to Crown corporations to protect jobs? It had nothing to do with good business decisions. It meant that the Government would pump in hundreds of millions of dollars. In fact, if we look at Canadair and de Havilland, it was not millions of dollars, it was billions of dollars to try to keep those companies

February 16, 1987
afloat. Surely to goodness we should not run the country in that manner any longer. We cannot continue to hold on to these companies just to keep those jobs.
The second example used by socialists is that if the Crown corporation is successful we should hold on to it and take all the revenue from it to reduce the deficit. That is contrary to the philosophy of the Conservative Party and of the Government. We made very clear during the last election campaign that we would divest ourselves of Crown corporations which have been nothing but a drain on us for many years. I am saying that the socialists are wrong on both counts.
Referring back to the de Havilland example, not many months ago people protested at the airport in Downsview. They said that they would lose their jobs, that the technology would be moved down to the United States, and that the place would be shut down. At that time 4,400 people were employed at de Havilland, and today it employs 5,200 people. It has hired an additional 800 people because the company which bought de Havilland is putting it on an even firmer footing than it was before. Rather than just maintaining the technology which de Havilland had before, it is bringing in new technology. It is now to put the turbo-prop engine into a water bomber which is probably one of the best water bombers in the world. It is to upgrade that technology, and there are 800 new jobs.
The other example about which I want to talk is Canadair. It has certainly maintained all the jobs. In fact, it has probably added a few. I do not have the latest statistics on that, but I am sure it will be very successful as the years go on.
I fail to understand why the socialists rail away about the idea of the Government of Canada, or any provincial Government in the country, wanting to grab all the resources, take risks with the private sector, and risk the money of private taxpayers. I think Canadian taxpayers have just about had their fill with regard to the mismanagement of many Crown corporations.
1 have about another 10 minutes left, but I see that it is almost one o'clock. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, may I call it one o'clock and return to my debate after lunch.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: WORLDWATCH INSTITUTE'S WARNING ON THREATS TO ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in its State of the World 1987 Report, the Worldwatch Institute warns that human use of the air, water, land, forests and other lifesupporting systems on earth may be pushing nature over thresholds beyond which it cannot absorb further use without permanent change and damage. The result has been contamination of the atmosphere, climatic change, a mass extinction of plant and animal species, the long term prospect of a decline in the quality of life. The most threatening of the threshold crossings are the depletion of the ozone layer, climate change, and the loss of biological diversity.
The report goes on to say that so many natural systems becoming unstable within a short period of time could result in economic and political pressures which, in turn, could overwhelm the capacity of governments and individuals to adjust adequately. Tackling environmental problems of global magnitude transcends national differences and policies. Governments and parliamentarians must move these issues to the top of their agenda in search of answers on which our survival depends.

subtopic: NEED FOR NATIONAL COMMEMORATION HOLIDAY
NEED FOR NATIONAL COMMEMORATION HOLIDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, the third Monday in February, is Heritage Day, a day when we have the opportunity to celebrate the achievements and traditions of Canada.
For many years the Heritage Canada Foundation has campaigned for a national heritage holiday. We need such a holiday to draw our attention, to focus our thoughts on our history, our traditions, on those parts of our past which require our attention today. The buildings, streets, and structures of our unique history define our character. Their preservation is in trust to us, as individuals. We cannot depend entirely on government to define what is worth preserving or to tell us what parts of our past must be erased.
Here in Ottawa we have seen in recent days how important can be the voice of individual Canadians when raised in defence of those small but beautiful parts of our history which official bodies sometimes overlook.
The battle to preserve our past will never be over, Mr. Speaker. Let us create a national heritage holiday to remind us that when we lose our past we lose an important part of what it means to be a Canadian today.
February 16, 1987

subtopic: EAST TIMOR-REPORTED MASSACRES BY INDONESIAN FORCES
EAST TIMOR-REPORTED MASSACRES BY INDONESIAN FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since 1975 Indonesia has illegally occupied the former Portuguese colony of East Timor. Amnesty International estimates that up to one-third of the East Timorese have been killed by Indonesian forces. Now there are reports that in August of last year the entire population of the village of Fo-Mano was massacred by Indonesian troops, and yet Canada has been very silent about these abuses.
In 1985-86 Canada provided over $77 million of bilateral assistance to Indonesia. We continue to issue permits for the export of military equipment, and we even sponsored an arms bazaar in Indonesia. This week when the Indonesian Foreign Minister visits Canada would be a good time for us to show that we cared for human rights by speaking out against Indonesia's wrongful occupation of East Timor and demanding that East Timorese be involved in U.N. consultations on their future.

subtopic: RESPONSIBILITY TO PROTECT AND ENRICH NATIONAL HERITAGE
RESPONSIBILITY TO PROTECT AND ENRICH NATIONAL HERITAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we celebrate Heritage Day, and we have been doing so on the third monday of February since 1973, when a proposal by the Heritage Canada Foundation unanimously received the support of the Members of the House of Commons.
The purpose of Heritage Day is to remind us of the riches of our Canadian heritage. It is a day to reflect on the achievements of past generations.
As the Member for a riding that saw the birth of French Canadian culture in North America, and I am of course referring to the Beaupre Coast and the lie d'Orleans, I would like to take this opportunity to remind all Quebecers and Canadians that in 1986, the historic quarter in Quebec City was added to UNESCO's list of world heritage sites. This official recognition has enhanced Quebec City's international standing, confirmed once again by the success of Rendez-vous '87.
Mr. Speaker, we must remember that it is up to each and every one of us to protect and enrich our common heritage for future generations.

subtopic: GASOLINE TAXES-OPPOSITION TO POSSIBLE INCREASE
GASOLINE TAXES-OPPOSITION TO POSSIBLE INCREASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) recently indicated that higher consumer taxes on gasoline and other petroleum products are again being considered by the Government. Canadians are already paying too much tax on gasoline. In fact, since the Conservatives took office in 1984, gasoline taxes have risen by 10 per cent.
The price of gasoline is now between 35 per cent and 45 per cent higher in Canada than it is in the United States, taking into account the exchange rate. This enormous price difference is hindering the growth of Canada's important tourism industry which employs over 600,000 Canadians. Considering that 74 per cent of Americans travel to Canada by automobile, it is easy to conclude that the price of gasoline is an important factor in their decision to visit Canada and in the length of time of their visits. I urge the Government to think twice before again raising gasoline taxes: think about tourism, and think about jobs, jobs, jobs.

subtopic: FIRST MEETING OF NATIONAL ADVISORY BOARD FOR SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
FIRST MEETING OF NATIONAL ADVISORY BOARD FOR SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first meeting of the Prime Minister's newly created National Advisory Board for Science and Technology took place this morning.
Significantly, the board is chaired by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and is composed of some of Canada's leading industrialists and scientists. I am pleased that Dr. Douglas Wright, President of the University of Waterloo, is a member of this prestigious board.
The establishment of the board was one of the major initiatives in the October Speech from the Throne. Pursuant to its mandate, this committee will assess national science and technology goals and policies and their application to Canada's economy. The Government has taken an incoherent set of programs left to us by the former administration and has created an organized science and technology strategy. These measures are designed to place Canada on the leading edge of high-technology competition, thereby maintaining and creating many new jobs and giving us one of the finest standards of living in the world.

February 16, 1987

subtopic: NEED FOR IMPROVED WEST COAST FACILITIES
NEED FOR IMPROVED WEST COAST FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Scotia Cape and seven of her crew members remain missing off the West Coast. Last week I drew to the attention of the House the need for improved search and rescue facilities. I renew that call today and draw to the attention of the House the dedication and bravery of those who continue to look for any sign of the ship and crew.
I take this opportunity as well to call on the Government to initiate long overdue safety measures for fishing vessels. It has been 11 years since British Columbia extended Workers' Compensation coverage to fishermen, yet there are still no federal regulations for safety in the workplace.
In consultation with fishermen and Vessel owners, the federal Government should move immediately to establish tests for vessel and load stability, gear inspection, vessel seaworthiness, and other safety regulations. Fishing remains one of the most dangerous occupations in Canada. Federal inspection of vessels and federal safety regulations are long overdue.

subtopic: FIRST MEETING OF NATIONAL ADVISORY BOARD FOR SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
FIRST MEETING OF NATIONAL ADVISORY BOARD FOR SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, another one of the major initiatives announced in the Government's Speech from the Throne has become a reality. The National Advisory Board for Science and Technology is holding its first meeting in Ottawa today. I would like to extend my best wishes to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who will chair this advisory board. I also congratulate Mr. Alex Curran and Dr. Steve Acres, two members appointed to the board from Saskatoon. They bring with them years of innovative experience in the business and scientific fields.
Saskatoon's advanced technology sector which involves biotechnology, electronics, and telecommunications has gained a reputation for excellence world-wide. Indeed, Saskatoon plays a creative role in contributing to the development of science and technology policies. I would like to congratulate the Government for constructing a new national consensus on science and technology, a consensus which will enhance our economy and build upon Canada's competitive strengths.

subtopic: OPENING OF PAROLE SUPERVISION FACILITY IN TORONTO
OPENING OF PAROLE SUPERVISION FACILITY IN TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the many, many promises the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made on behalf of the Conservative Party during the last election campaign was the promise to consult Canadians before taking decisions that would affect their lives. Whether it is a major international fishing treaty or the opening of a halfway house for parolees in Toronto, the record of the Government is an absolute and unmitigated disaster when it comes to consultation.
The Exodus-Link parole supervision facility in Toronto's Parkdale community is a case in point. They are picketing and signing petitions and threatening sit-ins.

subtopic: ROBERTSON DAVIES-RECIPIENT OF MEDAL OF HONOR FOR LITERATURE
ROBERTSON DAVIES-RECIPIENT OF MEDAL OF HONOR FOR LITERATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise today and advise the House of the great tribute paid in the United States to our great Canadian novelist, Robertson Davies. On February 24, at a dinner to be held in his honour, Mr. Davies, an internationally acclaimed novelist, will receive the 1987 Medal of Honor for Literature from the National Arts Club of New York City. Robertson Davies has provided many hours of enlightenment and enjoyment to Canadians from coast to coast and readers around the globe. I am sure all Members of the

subtopic: AUTOMATION OF LIGHTSTATIONS-CALL FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY
AUTOMATION OF LIGHTSTATIONS-CALL FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coastal residents have taken the Mulroney Government to task for automating West Coast light stations. Pierre Forand, a helicopter pilot and distinguished recipient of the Medal of Bravery, stated in a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney): "I am speaking from firsthand experience when I say that a manned light station provides this coast with a margin of safety that would be dangerously reduced if automation was to take place." Far from waking up and smelling the coffee, the Conservatives plan a further round of de-staffing for Green Island, Ivory, Lucy, and Addenbrook.
The Government and ministerial pencil pushers ignore the valuable work of light keepers. It appears the only thing they know about navigation is how to get to the parliamentary lounge. They argue for cost efficiency, yet ignore the high maintenance cost and frequent failure of automated equipment. They ignore the search and rescue work of lightkeepers because there is no job description for saving lives.
We hear of marine tragedies because of inadequate weather reporting, yet a Department of the Government denied a lightkeeper's request for weather recording equipment. Enough is enough. We must upgrade service instead of denigrating lightkeepers. Once again I call upon the Government to initiate a full public inquiry into the automation of lightsta-tions.

maintopic: INCREASED LUMBER EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES
INCREASED LUMBER EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as the Canadian lumber industry is concerned, the doom and gloom have become a boom. Just a few weeks ago media pundits and opposition Members were predicting the imposition of the export tax on softwood lumber would mean the loss of thousands of jobs and the closing of hundreds of mills. In fact Canadian lumber sales to the U.S. are more than holding up.
