There has been a tradition in North America and other western nations of recognizing the rights of capital investment, but we are sometimes rather slow in recognizing the rights of employees to a stake in their jobs. Often their jobs have been sold right out from under them. That has happened in some situations of privatization. It is good that in this particular case the principle that workers have a stake in their jobs was recognized.
While I was pleased that there was that protection for the rights of workers, that does not eliminate my major concern about this Bill which privatizes Teleglobe. It is important to try to see the issue in context, the context basically being the Conservative's ideological fixation with privatization. In the Budget Papers of May, 1985, we read:
In the process of rationalizing its corporate holdings in the future, the government will adopt a new approach based on the premise that a Crown corporation or other equity investment should be sold unless it is fulfilling a public policy purpose. This way, the government will return to the private sector activities that more properly belong there.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that Teleglobe, which is involved as a vital link in Canada's communications, is fulfilling a vital public policy purpose and that on that basis alone it should not be privatized.
On the next page the paper goes on to say:
Selling corporate interests will have a number of benefits. It will reduce the size of government in the economy and make room for private sector initiatives; it will improve market efficiency and the allocation of resources; it will improve firm efficiency through market discipline and by reducing political and bureaucratic impediments;
I would like to consider those. It says that it will reduce the size of government in the economy. Certainly Teleglobe is not that large a corporation, but selling it will to some extent reduce the size of government in the economy. We are dealing with an ideology that government involvement in the economy is somehow wrong. We have seen no studies which indicate the optimum size for government in the economy. How much does the Conservative Party want government in the economy to be reduced? What are the advantages of reducing government involvement in the economy? Those questions have not been answered. The Government says it will make room for private sector initiatives. I do not know what private sector initiatives will be involved in the sale of Teleglobe. It is being sold to a small company which is having a great deal of difficulty raising the money to purchase it, even at the fire sale price for which it is being sold.
The paper goes on to say that it will improve market efficiency and the allocation of resources. What market efficiency are we talking about here? We are dealing with a natural monopoly. I do not see any possibility of improving market efficiency by privatizing Teleglobe. With regard to the

February 16, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
allocation of resources, I am not sure what that has to do with the sale of Teleglobe.
The paper says that it will improve firm efficiency through market discipline. Again, Mr. Speaker, there is no market discipline in this particular case because we are dealing with a natural monopoly. The Bill itself grants an extension of the monopoly for a further five years, protected by law. Even apart from that protection of law, the nature of the enterprise means that there is not likely to be any competition. Therefore, in effect, there is no market discipline.
The paper also uses the words, "by reducing political and bureaucratic impediments". These are the kinds of code words which the Conservatives sometimes use to talk about the process of regulation. They see regulation as bureaucratic impediment to the proper operation of the market. Yet, at the same time as they are talking about privatizing Teleglobe they say that it will be regulated in the public interest, that it will be under the regulations of the CRTC. On the one hand the Conservative Party is saying that we must eliminate regulations, that they are acting as a strait-jacket for private enterprise, while on the other hand they are trying to assure the Canadian people that although something will be privatized it will be firmly regulated in the public interest. I have some difficulty with that kind of thinking.
As I look at the Government's guidelines, its statement of the purpose of privatization, I see no justification for the sale of Teleglobe, except the ideological one, that they want to reduce government involvement in the economy. It is a straight ideological decision and has nothing whatsoever to do with the pragmatic benefits which would possibly flow from privatization, as they are outlined in the policy paper.
I would like to say a little about the importance of Teleglobe. We are not talking about simply another Crown corporation which we can either have or not have, which does not really matter that much. We are talking about a very important link in Canada's communications industry. Teleglobe has responsibility for all overseas telecommunications entering and leaving Canada. It includes telephone, telegraph, cable and telex communications. It is a joint owner of submarine ocean cables and telecommunications satellite systems. On that basis it has had an effective monopoly on all overseas telecommunications.
Teleglobe has been a consistent moneymaker. It is for that reason that it has been referred to as the jewel of Crown corporations. In 1985 it recorded a profit of $53.2 million. That is money coming into the federal Treasury. The Conservatives are concerned about the deficit, as are we all. In 1985 Teleglobe brought in $53.2 million and that will happen over and over again. The Conservatives are like the rather foolish person in the fairy tale who wanted to kill the goose which laid the golden egg. When we have a revenue producer the Government wants to put it in the private market and let someone else have the revenue rather than allowing it to accrue in the public interest.
In fact, the ideological fixation of the Party which is, unfortunately, in Government at the present time seems to be the mind-set that there is only one thing worse than a Crown corporation that is losing money, and that is a Crown corporation that is making money. We are dealing here with a Crown corporation which is making money, and that is very clearly something the Government cannot stomach. It is something which has to be sloughed off to the private sector at whatever price.
In 1985, Teleglobe's total revenues were $678 million, and I will compare that later with the total revenues of Memotec, the company which is taking Teleglobe over. The former Minister, who had to resign while he is being investigated, was in charge. There was an offer of purchase and sale from British Telecom for $750 million. The Government turned that down, and rightly so. It said it did not want this vital industry to pass into non-Canadian hands, and I agree with the Government there. If it had sold Teleglobe to a non-Canadian company, I would have been very opposed, as would, I am sure, other members of my Party. However, that $750 million was a benchmark of value. It gives us some indication of what other people saw as the value of Teleglobe. But what did we finally receive for Teleglobe when it was sold to Memotec, the minnow which is trying to swallow a whale, as it was referred to by the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell)? The Government is fudging. It indicates it sold Teleglobe for some $608.3 million, but if we look into it a little more closely, we see this is not the case at all. Of that $608.3 million, $102 million is accumulated cash which the company has on hand. There is an additional $18 million dividend. When that is subtracted from the $608.3 million, it leaves $488.3 million which Memotec is reputed to have paid for Teleglobe. Even the amount of $488.3 million does not represent what Memotec is really paying, because in addition it is also taking over debt liabilities which amount to $143 million. What this means very clearly is that the Government will only receive $345 million for Teleglobe as no actual funds will be paid for the debt. The debt is simply something which will be carried on Teleglobe's books.
The Government talks about receiving $608 million for the sale of Teleglobe when in actual fact it will only receive $345 million. I refer again to the statement I made a little earlier that British Telecom was prepared to pay $750 million. Therefore, we have a sale at approximately half of what the Government could have gotten if it had been prepared to sell at the earlier price. The question is, why is the Government making this sale? We cannot see any justification whatsoever for this except that the Government has an ideological opposition to the very idea of keeping Teleglobe in public hands. It wants Teleglobe privatized. We are very concerned about the purchase price.
In addition, we are concerned about the way in which this whole contract was handled. The previous speaker, the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ravis), became a little
February 16, 1987

annoyed with my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway, for asking about the fact that trading had been suspended on Memotec. he said that any question of insider trading was pure speculation. Perhaps it is. Perhaps it is pure speculation. We do not have the facts. There is an investigation taking place and I think we all want to see what that investigation will reveal. There are some very interesting facts which are already known. On February 5, the day the Minister was advised that Memotec had won the bid, the stocks of Memotec jumped by $2.38 a share to a value of about $13 a share on the Toronto Stock Exchange. At that point the trading was halted, but it resumed the next day. More than half the number of the total shares traded in 1986 were traded in the next two days. Naturally, there have been questions raised, and not just by members of our Party and the Liberal Party, there have been very serious questions raised in the financial community as to whether or not there was insider trading. We are suggesting that before the Government proceeds with this sale, which we do not think is a very good sale even on the face of it, it should at least wait until the results of an investigation of Memotec trading has taken place. That is why we are moving that there be a halt put to the passage of this Bill, that the Bill be hoisted for a while.
Certainly, there are a number of issues which I have already delineated. We have very serious concerns about this Bill. The Financial Post has indicated there is a cloud over the deal. When trading in stock has been suspended, when the Government has had a series of scandals and near-scandals and allegations, some of which might not be founded in fact but which are putting a lot of pressure on the Government, I would think the Government itself would want to move as expeditiously as possible to clear up the total atmosphere which is undermining confidence in everything the Government is attempting to do. I would think the Government would not want to push through this particular Bill when all the questions which relate to its conduct in other areas leave the Government under a cloud, and there have been serious questions raised about insider training in this particular area.
In conclusion, I am very pleased that the Minister has indicated there are some guarantees for the pension rights and working conditions of the employees of Teleglobe. I think that is extremely important. I am glad to see that this is being looked after. We will be looking at that in committee to ensure that those rights are protected. At the same time, I cannot in any way give my support to a Bill which is selling off a public asset at a fire-sale price, which is taking a vital link in Canada's communications industry and placing it into private hands, when we do not see any justification for doing so. There is no justification in terms of the Government's own strategy and guidelines for what privatization is all about. I am at a complete loss to understand why the Government is proceeding with this Bill at a time when there is so much concern about the possibility of insider trading and all the other questions being raised about the Government's integrity at the present time.

Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker), and I listened very attentively to what she said. In her remarks she indicated that the Government had to sell Crown corporations because of the fact that we have some financial difficulty and because of the fact that the deficit is high. She did not quite say that it had to be sold to pay off the national debt, but the implication was clearly there that the Government sees what it is doing, the selling of the assets of Canadians to pay for its mismanagement, as being appropriate. It is a little like someone selling the furniture to pay the rent. It is not the correct approach. Perhaps the Government feels that this corporation does not fulfil an important policy objective. By the way, I have yet to see the Government's communications policy. I would like to know what it is and what are its intentions for the long term. The Government should bring forward a policy and say that it is a policy Canadians have discussed. Then, after it had been discussed and adopted, the Government could say that it feels a particular Crown corporation is no longer required to fulfil that policy objective. If that were the case, we could proceed with the sale, provided that we did not give it away, that it was sold at an appropriate price.
I do not think we sold the company for a very high price, but we did not quite give it away, as was suggested by a member of the New Democratic Party. Obviously when one takes over the liabilities of a company, it must be considered part of the purchase cost. However, even taking that into account, we must remember that it was not sold for a very high price. The point I am making this afternoon is that we should have established the communications policy of the Government. Then we could decide whether or not the Crown corporation fulfilled that policy objective, whether or not it was necessary. If the Government indicated that it had a policy and that the corporation was not required to fulfil that policy, perhaps it would have been all right to sell it off. I do not have a mental block about selling everything or not selling anything. However, there are Crown corporations which should be kept by the Government. We should not sell them all because it is the "in" thing to do.
Teleglobe Canada
We must remember that a Conservative Prime Minister of Canada, Sir John A. Macdonald, and the other Fathers of Confederation inserted the issue of a national railway in the Constitution. We should also remember that having government corporations or national corporations is not something which should be foreign to Conservative Members of Parliament. It is something that has been with us all along, something strongly supported by past Conservative administrations.
My colleagues in the NDP want to sell hardly anything in the way of Crown corporations. I do not know for a fact that they would not sell anything, but generally they are not in favour of the Government divesting itself of any Crown corporation. However, members on the government side generally want to sell everything, whether or not it fulfils an objective, whether or not it is a good price, and so on, just because they have a bent that it is the correct thing to do.
I say to Hon. Members on both sides of the House that the merits of Crown corporations must be looked at individually. I would say, for example, that Petro-Canada is very necessary, and there are many others. I happen to think that our national airline is a very necessary Crown corporation. Nevertheless, until we determine what is needed in order to fulfil the policy objective of the Government, we should not proceed with the sale of Teleglobe Canada. It is being done in a backward manner. What will happen in a year or two? Will the Government decide that because of some new policy objective we have to buy it back? We do not know. Are we to sell it and then realize that we should not have done so? It will be too late then.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in today's debate on Bill C-38, the Bill to privatize Teleglobe. It has been very interesting listening to the debate on this particular issue over the last two days. It appears as though the position of the Liberal Party would be privatization if necessary but not necessarily privatization. That would seem fairly consistent with the Liberal Party's position on free trade and NATO. Liberals really cannot make up their minds about their position. Unfortunately, I did not have the opportunity of asking the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) just what the criteria for privatization would be and how the Liberal Party would apply those criteria to the 11 Crown corporations this Government has privatized over the past two years.
I understand that the NDP's philosophy is basically consistent and would appear to be totally against privatization. From listening to the debate, one might feel that it believes that if a Crown corporation is making money, the Government should keep it and should be in the business of making money. As far as the Progressive Conservative Party is concerned, that is just not the purpose of government. We are not in government to run business, we are in Government to govern the country.
Perhaps it would be appropriate to look at the record of privatization. During the 1984 election campaign, I and many of my colleagues heard our constituents say that they felt the Government should get out of many Crown corporations which were more appropriately run by free enterprise. That was certainly my view, and I made a commitment to my constituents that I would work hard to pressure the Government to undertake a program of the privatization of Crown corporations that no longer met a public policy objective.
Indeed, in November 1984, just two months after we took office, a paper entitled A New Direction for Canada: An Agenda for Economic Renewal was published. I am proud to say that this Government has followed that agenda. One of the objectives outlined in it was and remains the improved management of Crown corporation assets.
In the Budget of May 1985, concrete plans were announced for the rationalization and privatization of Crown corporations and other federal investments, such as those mentioned by the Minister earlier including federal buildings, based on the premise that those corporations or investments should be sold or wound up if public ownership is no longer necessary to meet public policy objectives. Our philosophy has been very clear.
In the implementation of that objective, the record is clear. We have already privatized 11 Crown corporations beginning in July 1985 with the completion of the sale of Northern Transportation Company Limited. We have done this in a pragmatic way. In fact, I am sometimes pressured about moving more quickly. We realize, however, that many interests must be met. There are the interests of consumers and there are the interests of employees. That was certainly an issue with

February 16, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
respect to the sale of de Havilland. There is also the interest of the public at large. All of those interests are ones with which the Government must deal.
I know that the Minister responsible for privatization has, with her officials, been undertaking a solid program of evaluating each Crown corporation to see whether or not they meet the criteria which have been set and to see if it is time to seek out private owners. We are making considerable progress in this respect. I think that Teleglobe is perhaps the largest such sale to date.
Why do we think it is important to sell back to the private sector these corporations which, in the view of the Government and in the view of the public at large, no longer serve to fulfil the necessary public policy objective? When we sell something back to the private sector, we free it from many of the constraints inevitably involved in Government. These restraints, I know, sometimes frustrate many of us, but they are there. They are necessary for organizations of the Government because there are many considerations which come into account. Crown corporations cannot respond quickly to market initiatives. Of course, in many cases there is a requirement for new capital. New capital would allow a company like Teleglobe to expand, and the Government itself is not an appropriate source for this kind of capital investment. I do not think that is what the taxpayers want the Government to do.
Once a corporation is sold and if it is well operated and soundly managed, it will be able to raise capital for expansion from individual Canadians, pension funds and investors. It will be able to expand and operate in a much more effective and efficient manner, free of the burden of bureaucracy. That of course is what the Government and our Party believe.
We are not alone in this belief. It has been extremely interesting to learn that over the last two years, the philosophy of this Progressive Conservative Government has been shared by many western European Governments, Governments of a variety of political stripes. In Great Britain, the sale of British Gas was a tremendous success story. It was considered to be a rather staid company, but it has now been sold and it is doing tremendously well. The same is true of British Telecom. Of course, very recently the announcement of the sale of British Airways was made. Last night's Venture program on CBC indicated that this announcement was accompanied by fireworks. It reminded me of Expo 86. The announcement was certainly made in a very outgoing way and there was a tremendous response.
It is also interesting to note that in many cases, when Crown corporations are sold to the public, the value of their shares go up very quickly. I think this was a point made by my hon. friend from Mississauga. When a corporation is sold to the public, the public becomes interested and gets involved. In fact, in Britain they are talking about the people's capitalism, the opportunity for the people of Britain to invest and become involved in companies which were formerly controlled by the Government. It has been a very successful venture.
France has followed a similar course. Under the previous socialist Government of France, as I am sure my colleagues in the NDP are aware, the sale of many Crown corporations was undertaken. Many of the largest corporations in the auto glass, chemicals and telecommunication industries were nationalized in 1982 and are now being offered for sale. The present Government of France is carrying on with that initiative as well and it has been very successful.
As my colleague mentioned earlier today, even in Spain with the socialist Government which has been in office since October 1982, some state-run companies are being offered for sale. It is becoming accepted by Governments on both sides of the political spectrum that the Government should get out of running businesses as these businesses may operate much more effectively in the private sector.
I know that my colleagues in the New Democratic Party of Canada simply are not up to date and in tune with global thinking on these issues. That is not surprising because NDP Members are not even in tune with their NDP colleagues in British Columbia on such issues as the 15 per cent export tax on forestry products. Perhaps they should begin to listen to their colleagues around the country and around the world. They might get updated on these issues.
Having discussed the principle of privatization, I would like to turn to the specific project that is at hand, the sale of Teleglobe. Over the last two days, I have not heard very much about the background of Teleglobe. I have a particular interest in it. I am sure my colleagues are aware that the Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Company which was founded in 1949 acquired the assets of Cable and Wireless Ltd. and Canadian Marconi Ltd., both privately-operated British firms. When my father first came to Canada in the early 1900s after serving in the First World War, he worked for Cable and Wireless Ltd. and I remember as a child hearing stories about that company. My uncle worked for them, too. He was in South America. I remember the stories of the laying of the cables across the Atlantic, so I have a kind of special interest in this issue.
In 1949, the COTC was formed, and in 1956 the first longdistance multi-purpose coaxial submarine cable was laid across the Atlantic Ocean between Scotland and Newfoundland. That brought in a new era of long-distance calling. Then the name was changed to Teleglobe. It has been a very successful company performing important service in long-distance telecommunications, working both with the telephone companies in providing the cable and the system for overseas telephone calls, and the telex systems as well. I thought it was interesting that its assets are spread right across the country. It has three major categories of assets. It shares with a number of foreign entities ownership in a number of transoceanic submarine cables most of which form part of the Commonwealth cable system. It also owns approximately 3 per cent of Intelsat which operates communications satellites around the
February 16, 1987

globe. Earth stations operating with the Intelsat system are located in Nova Scotia, Quebec and Vancouver Island. Those are wholly owned by Teleglobe. It also operates international switching centres or gateways in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver where overseas traffic is routed to and from the networks of Canada's domestic carriers. The company has certainly expanded its operations and performed a very important service, and I would like to congratulate those involved for the excellent service.
My colleague who spoke before me said that this sale is a good deal. It is. It is a good deal for the seller, the buyer, consumers, and the country as a whole. The Toronto Sun is not often complimentary about this Government but even that paper, in its editorial yesterday, said that Memotec appears to be a good deal for both the seller, which is the taxpayer, and the buyers, which are some of biggest pension funds around. The editorial said it was time to applaud a move that will bring major benefits to just about everyone. I think that when you can manage a situation like that it is almost miraculous.
Let me just reiterate some of the benefits. As Chairman of the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the interest of consumers is very near and dear to my heart. This is a particularly good deal for consumers. As you know, as part of the sale of Teleglobe there is an agreement that overseas rates will be reduced by 13 per cent on January 1, 1988, and telex charges will decline by 10 per cent. Those are very significant amounts. Many Canadians call their families and friends overseas. For the average Canadian family who would like to call their relatives or friends on an anniversary, a birthday or even in an emergency, as well as the inevitable long-distance calls at Christmas, this means their 1988 phone bill could fall by around $50. Has anyone thought about that? It is like a tax break. We have many wonderful Filipino Canadians and if they call home the savings will be even greater. These are real savings that Canadians will enjoy as a result of this sale.
That does not even take into account the very positive impact for the small business person operating a telex. I have many business people like this in my own riding, and for them the savings could run in the hundreds of dollars. At the same time we have the assurance for the first time that Teleglobe will come under the jurisdiction of the CRTC. It will be a privately-operated and publicly-regulated company. We know that the company will have to show its costs and will be held to an appropriate rate of return. Consumers will have the opportunity to review those figures at CRTC hearings. Earlier today a Member on the other side of the House said that after five years prices will increase. I would say the exact opposite. For the first time we will have a greater degree of control over long-distance calling and telex rates.
There has been a lot of discussion as well about the sale price. I would like to put the facts on the record. The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) said when he spoke on the Bill on Friday that all we were getting was $350 million. That is totally wrong. I am not surprised because

Mr. Speaker, I have a comment to make and a couple of questions to ask of the speaker. On the issue of the treatment of employees the member has said how well protected the employees will be. The Member referred to rate reductions. The cost of making overseas calls and telex calls will be reduced. Does the Member not realize that Teleglobe had already planned rate reductions? The only way in which the company can survive is with a measure of protection. We are not talking about some free enterprise company in the private sector beating all the competition, but about a highly protected company. This makes it quite different from what she is talking about, a thriving private sector as opposed to the public sector. This area will have to be protected if it is going to survive at all. You cannot have it both ways. Mr. Speaker, on the first point, the Government does listen to all groups. That is vital to governing. We listen to representations made from all quarters. That is a credit to all who have been involved.
I was a little surprised by the Member's last comment that the alternative would be to leave the market totally open to the U.S. I know of my hon. colleague's very great concern about the protection of Canadian culture and Canadian industry. However, we rejected that possibility because we felt that it was in the best interests of Canada that the company remain in Canadian control. Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a couple of comments and ask a question of the Hon. Member. I think she may be guilty of making some statements which disturb me and could leave misleading impressions with people viewing these debates. I suggest that she should get her facts straight.
I am disturbed by her comments and some of those of her colleagues about the lumber deal. She knows perfectly well that members of the New Democratic Party in British Columbia have been saying for years that it is about time that B.C. started to charge adequate stumpage rates on its forests. They have taken that position consistently for a long time. However, they agree with us that Canada should not be forced into a situation of imposing a lumber tax because of American actions. In effect, we should have the right to be wrong in this country. My colleagues in British Columbia happen to agree with that.
However, now that the Conservatives have fallen into third place in the polls, they seem to be directing their fire toward the New Democrats. I guess they cannot forgive us for moving into the number two position. We are going to go a bit higher, too. That was, perhaps, a digression.
My specific point is that the Hon. Member reiterates that this is a $600 million sale. First, $102 million of the proceeds which the Government is drawing from this sale is money which it has drawn from Teleglobe Canada by means of a cash distribution without the need to sell the company at all. The Hon. Member will, of course, agree with me that that figure is outstanding on the balance sheet of the company. It was cash reserves or reserves in short-term investments and there was no need to sell Teleglobe, but the Government wanted $100 million to bring the deficit down for the Budget of the Finance Minister (Mr. Wilson) later this week.
In addition, as the member knows, there is an $18 million dividend which is also being paid just prior to the sale being consummated. The real question is that of the $142 million in debt liabilities. We have talked to the President of Memotec
February 16, 1987

who has confirmed that as part of the purchase price Memotec is assuming Teleglobe's debt liability which amounts to $143 million. This means that the Government will only receive $345 million for Teleglobe as no actual funds will be paid for the debt. It is simply a transfer of responsibility for the debt from the present owner, the Government of Canada, to the new owner, Memotec. I would like the Hon. Member to confirm that that effectively means that all the cash Memotec has to come up with is approximately $345 million. There is room for misunderstanding here. I would not want the Hon. Member to be guilty of promulgating misunderstanding.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments on this Bill. I would say quite honestly that I am open to stand corrected op this particular point. I think it is something which will have to be looked into in some detail because the difference of $ 140 million between what the Hon. Member contends is being paid for Teleglobe and what we think it is, after conversation with the President of Memotec, is a very substantial difference. In fact, it is a very material difference indeed. It concerns me that in the process of privatization, the Government, a bit like its predecessor in office, one might say, is more concerned about the PR value of this particular act of Government than about the real facts.
I have just taken the trouble to look through the information kit which was distributed by the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall) in order to try to get an answer to this particular question. I was concerned when I looked at the notes of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), who, I assure the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins), will definitely be back in the House of Commons after the next election. He may not have the pleasure of her company, but he will be back.
This question is very serious. I was involved as the critic with respect to the privatization of both Canadair and de Havilland, and when we analysed the obligations which were being assumed by the Government, we found in fact that we effectively paid the private sector to purchase and take over those two particular corporations. Then, of course, in the case of Canadair, the Government, by the awarding of contracts, has taken effective action to ensure a better employment base for Canadair. That is good in terms of the aerospace industry
Teleglobe Canada
and the region of Montreal. However, the Hon. Member's suggestion that this is the virtue of private sector management is a bunch of hogwash. The fact is that government action, in terms of awarding a very important defence contract, has been the key action in securing the fortunes of Canadair, and it is quite possible that if that contract had been awarded to Canadair prior to the privatization taking place, the market value of the company, on its being privatized, would be considerably greater than it was at the time the company was sold.
We are going to have a lot of debate on these issues over the course of the next year or two. I might perhaps just say to those people who have come home from work, or those students who are watching the House of Commons for a few minutes before they turn to their homework or to watching Much Music, that when they hear members of the Progressive Conservative Party talking about the free market system, they should be aware that they are talking about something which makes them feel warm and cuddly. Given their status in the polls these days, the Conservatives have need of something which makes them feel good about themselves. There has not been a lot of good news for them over the course of the last four or five weeks.
The facts are that Teleglobe in being privatized, is certainly, and by no means, going into the free market system. This is a leverage buy-out in which a small company, which has only been listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange a couple of years, is paying a substantial price in terms of its resources in order to take over Teleglobe, but in doing so is being guaranteed by the Government a number of things which will ensure it will not have to function in the free market for at least the next five years, and possibly for some lengthy period of time beyond that. Teleglobe is the only international carrier of communications such as telephone, telex, and those kinds of communications, with Canada. It is a part of international treaties which give Canada access to the Intelsat satellite network. That status will continue for at least the next five years.
Teleglobe will be regulated in its profits. That means two things; first, it will be regulated in terms of not earning too much and, second, it will be permitted to have profits to ensure it does not earn too little. Therefore, in that sense it will not be in the free market. The telephone companies, which I think reacted perhaps irresponsibly, suggested they might find means of bypassing the services of Teleglobe Canada. They have been warned that legislation will be presented and adopted by the Government, presuming it maintains its majority, which will prevent the private sector companies from bypassing Teleglobe and routing overseas telephone calls through the United States. The American Government has effectively sought to break the internationally agreed to monopoly on international telecommunications through Intelsat and is setting up its own satellites in its place, if it can get them up in the air. Teleglobe Canada is also being told it has to maintain its role as Canada's participant in Intelsat so,

February 16, 1987
Automotive Strategy
therefore, it is being maintained in a very much regulated environment.
There is a strong case for Teleglobe staying as a regulated entity. Let us consider the situation in other countries. When the United Kingdom privatized British Telecom, it kept about 49 per cent ownership and a controlling interest in government hands. Then there are countries such as Australia, New Zealand, and France, which now have a Government which is friendly to Prime Minister Thatcher and President Reagan. West Germany also has a Government which is on the right rather than the left of the spectrum. There is Italy, Norway and Sweden. All of these countries with Governments, some of which are to the right, some of which are to the left, have in fact maintained their international telecommunications systems in government control. The British Government has kept British Telecom under government control as well, although just under 50 per cent has been privatized in terms of control. Why is that? I suggest it is because they have seen that there are good and proper reasons, and reasons which must be seriously considered, why one cannot have a totally free market in terms of international telecommunications.
If the Government really wanted to go that route, then Canada should have notified the other signatories that we are withdrawing from the Intelsat Treaty which, among other things, would have meant that we would be contributing, as the Americans are,to a very large increase in the cost of telecommunications for developing countries around the world which benefit from the Intelsat arrangements. We should have decided that we would have given free range to the telephone companies to route their calls through the United States, or through any other means they could find available, to use private sector or pirate satellites as they begin to get thrown up into the ionosphere. That is what the free market would be all about. The Government knows, as we know in this Party-but the Government will not say it and we will-that that kind of situation would have wreaked havoc in terms of any kind of reasonable and fair access to telecommunications for an awful lot of Canadians. Once we did that internationally, very quickly we would face the same kind of pressure to do it nationally as well. The result would be that my constituents in Ottawa Centre would find that their telephone rates to Vancouver, to Toronto to Montreal and abroad might drop quite drastically. They would benefit. However, the people living in Inuvik and up in the riding of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry) and my colleagues from northern Quebec, would have found an enormous increase in the cost of their telecommunications.
We do have cross-subsidization in this country and we need it if we are going to deal equitably in terms of access to communications for every Canadian. I think the Government surreptitiously recognizes that fact but publicly tells us that this is all for the free market. I am suggesting that that is a code word. It is designed to please the people of the National Citizens Coalition. This privatization stuff is only limited privatization and I want to suggest, as my colleagues have
suggested, that a company which is earning $50 million a year in profits could be making a substantial ongoing contribution to the cost of government services rather than selling the Crown jewel as we have in this case, for what may be as little as $350 million.
I may wish to continue my contribution to this debate when debate resumes tomorrow.
