subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING AN AUTOMOTIVE STRATEGY
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING AN AUTOMOTIVE STRATEGY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation in order to establish an automotive strategy for Canada based on the policy derived from "An Automotive Strategy for Canada", a report by the Federal Task Force on the Canadian Motor Vehicle and Automotive Parts Industries, which would not change the terms or spirit of the Canada-United States Automotive Products Trade Agreement, but would continue to limit the importation of certain motor vehicles and ensure that all motor vehicle manufacturers, who sell motor vehicles in the Canadian market, provide employment and create value within that market, commensurate with the benefits that they derive from it, and be required to produce Canadian content equal to at least sixty per cent (60%) of their sales in Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to bring this motion before the House today. However, it gives rise to extreme disquiet and concern in the automotive communities right across the country. That is what motivates my bringing it forward.
In 1983 we received a report which represented the views of both the unions and the companies within the industry. The report set out the serious future prospects and problems of the auto industry. The report was not acted upon by the previous Government. It went to the next Government, which also refused to act on it. I bring the motion before the House today because, first, it seems to me urgent that the House have a chance to debate what is a dire crisis emerging for the auto industry and, second, because it is a potential solution for the crisis.
We have just finished a series of hearings with representatives from the various parts of the auto industry, including the workers, as well as the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Cote) who appeared before us this afternoon.
February 16, 1987

In the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade we have begun to get into the debate. This motion comes at a particularly opportune time in response to some of the feelings and divisions which have arisen in the debate as reflected in the committee. It is now in order to bring it to the floor of the Elouse of Commons.
It is essential that the House and the country understand that we are talking about a crisis, an economic crisis which could cost the country, we have been told in testimony, up to 40,000 direct jobs. The reason for this is that we have created one set of conditions for those companies which have traditionally produced cars in this country. Under the Auto Pact they produce at a value of 60 per cent Canadian content.
However, there is a second set of companies, a set of Japanese and Korean companies, which have not made a commitment to that 60 per cent Canadian value added. If there is a shift in purchases from one set of companies to the other and if there is a set of increased imports by the year 1990, we are likely to see a tremendous over-capacity, perhaps up to three million cars in North America, which will inevitably force companies to start shutting down their operations. This will happen not just in the United States, where Chrysler recently took action, but increasingly so in Canada.
The crisis is there. It is there with respect to the people who talked to us from St. Catharines and from St. Thomas last week. Specifically, they suggested that a shift could be eliminated to the St. Thomas plant and cost within the next three to four months something up to 1,500 jobs just in the one community.
There are solutions. This motion tries to set out some of the solutions, drawing on the 1983 report. First, we must obtain a commitment from the Asian producers so that we have some type of balanced playing-field. We need a commitment to 60 per cent Canadian value added from their plants as well as from the Big Four. Second, in order to reach this commitment we have to be prepared to use, with force, the quotas which are quite legitimately in place for us to use under the GATT. We have to be prepared to say to the Japanese and the Koreans: "If you are not prepared to accept these commitments, which have been accepted by the other companies, then we will have to impose quotas on you".
We have to commit ourselves to the maintenance of the safeguards in the Auto Pact as it stands at the moment. There are many ancillary parts to the auto trade upon which it is impossible to sit down and talk on a bilateral basis with the United States. However, if we get ourselves into a position in which we are prepared to negotiate away that 60 per cent safeguard, then we are committing economic suicide so far as central Canada is concerned.
It is not just central Canada which is concerned. This is a point I want to stress. Throughout the country there are at this stage something close to 450,000 workers who depend on the auto industry. They do not live just in central Canada. They are spread out across the country. They come from all the
Automotive Strategy
different sectors of the economy, including the steel, petroleum, plastics, chemical and tire sectors. They form the heart of our economy as it exists across the country. This is not an Ontario issue, or an issue that belongs to Quebec. It is an issue that cuts right across Canada.
In conclusion, we are a small country that faces a very tough world today with respect to automotive competition. In order to succeed in that tough world, we need to have a strategy which is tough and effective, and a strategy which we have tried to outline in this motion today.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Kilgour (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING AN AUTOMOTIVE STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion of the Hon. Member who just spoke could be fairly summarized by saying that it calls for an automobile strategy for Canada. It also states that all motor vehicle manufacturers should be required to produce Canadian content equal to at least 60 per cent of their sales in Canada.
The Government is fully aware of the immense contribution that has been made by the Canadian automobile manufacturing industry to the economy of Canada. We know how many men and women work in the industry, and as the Member said, not only in southern Ontario but in other parts of Canada, including Quebec. Indeed, in western Canada we wish we had more manufacturing in that industry.
Our support for an efficient and internationally strong automotive industry has been unwavering. I wish to take the opportunity to tell Members of the House that over the next several months the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Cote) will be consulting with representatives of the auto industry and labour to examine current and important issues which bear upon the future viability of the auto sector.

As a matter of fact, he has already met with representatives of the Automobile Parts Manufacturers Association, the Canadian Auto Workers, and the Motor Vehicle Manufacturers' Association to begin discussions and explore possible solutions to different concerns identified by the industry. During these consultations, the Canadian content issue in the automobile industry is likely to be raised.
The Government's policy has always been to encourage a higher Canadian content rather than to set a definite percentage based on the automobile industry output. At the international level, any legislation requiring a precise Canadian content would go against our multilateral commercial commitments under GATT. Beside these trade related arguments, to require a certain level of Canadian content would not necessarily guarantee additional permanent jobs which is our main concern. That is the essential. Several factors seem to indicate that such measures would result instead in a reduction of Canada's competition in this industry. The gains made recently by the Canadian Automobile Industry in the areas of productivity and competition stem to a large extent from the

February 16, 1987
Automotive Strategy
individual reaction of each corporation to international competition. The increased competition within the industry has resulted in significant changes in the area of production and finished products, thereby improving Canada's competitive position.

The industry is undergoing immense structural changes. Around the globe automobile manufacturers and markets have become exceedingly competitive. I regret that the fierce level of world competition has meant that North American manufacturers have lost some of their traditional market share to imported vehicles. The new Asian manufacturers that are now establishing on this continent are bringing additional competitive pressures to bear on the domestic industry.
The Government has taken the position that the automobile industry must adopt new manufacturing technologies which are basic to world cost competitiveness. Therefore, the government policies are meant to encourage the adaptation of the Canadian automotive industry to meet those demands. For its part, the Government negotiated export restraint arrangements with Japan in order to provide the North American producers with a "breathing space". That action also served to prevent the diversion of Japanese vehicles through the United States and into the Canadian market.
The second step, the duty-free status which applies to vehicles currently imported from countries such as Korea and Mexico, was eliminated in the May 1985 Budget. That measure became effective January 1, 1987. The Government has also made efforts to ensure that Canada receives its proportionate share of Japanese investment in North America. Until recently, the majority of North American Asian investment has been made in the United States. Without our share of this new investment, as the Hon. Member for Essex- Windsor (Mr. Langdon) knows, the Canadian industry would have been faced with the prospect of lagging technological development and, as important, Japanese companies would have been able to import vehicles from their new United States plants, increase their penetration into the Canadian market, and yet make no significant contribution to our economy.
Since 1982, Japanese companies have made large investments in the North American assembly facilities. In Canada, Honda and Toyota have announced Canadian assembly investments amounting to $600 million. The GM/Suzuki project will add a further $500 million of direct investment, and Hyundai is planning to invest $300 million in an assembly plant near Montreal. These projects, and similar ones in the United States, will result in an additional annual production capacity in North America of 2.1 million units, of which some 480,000 units will be produced in Canada. These planned investments in Canada should result in an estimated 5,000 new direct jobs, and at least an equal number of indirect jobs.
In our discussions with Japanese and Korean automobile investors, the Government always stresses the importance of the objectives and performance requirements of the Auto Pact
and our desire to have companies that participate in the Canadian market contribute to the Canadian economy. Joining the Auto Pact is not mandatory, but all new entrants including Toyota, Honda, and Hyundai have publicly indicated that they plan to achieve Auto Pact status. It is expected that the GM/Suzuki joint venture will achieve Auto Pact status virtually from the start of production.
Nevertheless, the Government recognizes that, at the start, Asian assembly operations will require less labour and will be more dependent on parts supplied from offshore companies than is the case for the domestic vehicle manufacturers. For this reason, from the beginning, the Government has worked to ensure that these companies maximize Canadian value added in assembly operations with the objective of meeting Auto Pact status within a reasonable time frame.
Developing sound, long-term relationships with suppliers requires a determined effort. Over time, we believe that exciting opportunities for Canadian auto parts companies will arise. Canadian parts companies are well positioned to supply the new assemblers, and the Government is actively supporting Canadian manufacturers in their efforts to identify products and develop links with Japanese, European, and Korean assemblers. Opportunities also exist for foreign assemblers and suppliers to establish parts facilities in Canada either independently, or through joint ventures with Canadian producers. Although actual direct parts investment remains small, Toyota has constructed an aluminum wheel plant in British Columbia. As of this time, Japanese and Canadian parts manufacturers have formed 10 joint venture companies to produce a range of automotive components ranging from instrument panels to seat belts. Canadian companies have also entered into joint ventures with European partners to produce a range of sophisticated parts and components.
It is important to recognize the contribution that North American producers have made to our economy. Over the past five years, these companies have made massive capital investments to improve process technology, and to introduce new product lines while continuing to reduce costs. From 1980 to 1985, domestic vehicle assemblers averaged over $550 million annually in capital expenditures in Canada. American Motors is well advanced in the construction of a $760 million state of the art vehicle assembly plant in Brampton. That plant will have a world product mandate to produce 150,000 intermediate size cars per year. General Motors has chosen Canada as the site for one of its most significant investments- the Autoplex project. This $2 billion investment will produce a new line of GM-10 front-wheel drive cars. Of course GM is also undertaking the $500 million GM-Suzuki project to introduce a new line of small cars. Chrysler and Ford have also made impressive investments in their Canadian operations, directed mostly to robotics and plant automation. These companies are either producing or will produce very competitive products such as the Chrysler Van from Windsor, the Premier from Brampton, and General Motors new GM-10 car from Oshawa.
February 16, 1987

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING AN AUTOMOTIVE STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the auto industry is central to the health of the Canadian economy. One job in every seven is dependent upon the auto industry in Canada. This means that there is no part of Canada which can accept with equanimity any weakness or deterioration in the Canadian auto industry. No matter how remote any part of the country may think it is from those parts of central Canada where most of the automotive assembly or parts plants are found, its health and well-being are in fact linked with the auto industry.
Whether we are talking about the mining of iron ore, the manufacture of steel, textiles, or even forest products, to a very major degree their health and well-being are linked to the health and well-being of our auto industry. This is why it is essential for the Government to have a clear and definite strategy to preserve and strengthen the Canadian auto industry.
One element of the strategy must be to ensure that the Auto Pact and its safeguards are not allowed to be up for grabs in the current United States-Canada free trade negotiations. In spite of questions posed to the Government in the House very regularly, there is still an area of doubt about its real intentions, created by the lack of firmness and precision in the answers given by government Ministers to these questions about whether the Auto Pact is or is not, will or will not be on the free trade negotiating table.
Last Friday, speaking at a University of Windsor seminar, Gordon Richie, chief deputy trade negotiator to Simon Reisman, Canada's representative at the free trade talks, said the following, as reported in the the Windsor Star.
-the Auto Pact isn't excluded by the Canadian Government, as cultural sovereignty and national security matters are.
Everything else, he said, is on the bargaining table, and of the Auto Pact he said: "We're always open to suggestions".
But when asked to state the Government's intentions, Richie replied: "I can tell you my clear understanding, and the mandate governing us in the talks, is we have not raised the Auto Pact, the Americans have not raised the Auto Pact. Neither the Americans nor Canadians have raised the Auto Pact, and for our part we don't see any pressing need for it to be raised".
I repeat, however, Mr. Richie said the Auto Pact was not excluded in advance from the free trade talks in the same way that the Government claims cultural sovereignty and national security matters have been excluded.
The lead story in today's edition of The Financial Post reported that U.S. trade negotiator Peter Murphy appears to be readying himself to propose major changes to the Canada-U.S. Auto Pact, and that he intends to put these changes on the table this coming March. Therefore, we need a clear declaration by the Government, which we have not as yet received, that as part of its strategy to preserve the auto industry, so fundamental to the well-being of the Canadian economy, the Auto Pact will not be on the table and that its safeguards will not be on the table no matter what Mr. Murphy intends to bring forward in March.
Automotive Strategy
There is a risk that the Auto Pact is up for grabs in the free trade negotiations, that the Auto Pact itself or its key safeguards will be traded off, perhaps with the best intentions on the part of the Government, to get something else it considers important to the economy. The risks are there so long as the Auto Pact is on the table, along with everything else which is allowed to be on the table in the free trade negotiations.
There seems to be some pressure growing in the United States for changes to be made to the Auto Pact. These pressures are based upon a very fundamental misconception. Some people in the United States seem to think that the problems they have and the problems they foresee with their auto industry are linked with the operations of the Canada-U.S. Auto Pact.
As part of the strategy which the Government must have to preserve the health of our auto industry, it must make it clear to the United States and its people that any problems they have or they foresee in their auto industry have nothing to do with trade between Canada and the United States in the automotive sector. Instead, that trade, developed and enhanced under the Canada-U.S. Auto Pact over the past 20 years, has helped to build and strengthen the United States auto industry.
We must ensure that the Americans understand that hundreds of thousands of jobs in that country are dependent upon the continued existence of the Canada-U.S. Auto Pact and its safeguards in their current form. If the safeguards and that pact are allowed to be weakened in the free trade negotiations or otherwise, those hundreds- of thousands of American jobs are in peril. Their future existence cannot be ensured.
We must also remind the Americans that for 13 years of the 20 years the Auto Pact has been in existence the Americans had a surplus. It is only in the last four or five years that the balance has shifted in the other direction. Surely it is not the American definition of a fair deal to be one in which only the American side can ever benefit. Surely any deals we have with the Americans and with other countries in the world must be deals where both sides win. Surely that is the experience of the Canada-U.S. Auto Pact.
We must ensure that the Americans recognize-and we must recognize it as well-that if there are problems emerging in the auto industries in both countries, they have nothing to do with the Canada-U.S. Auto Pact which, as I said, has worked to strengthen those industries. Instead, they have arisen out of the problems created by the import of cars from Japan and Korea. These problems are also developing, strangely enough and paradoxically enough, from the investments by Japan and Korea in Canada and the United States in new assembly plants. These plants will not be creating the same number of jobs as have equivalent plants built by North American producers, for a simple reason-Japanese and Korean producers in Canada with one exception, have not been compelled by the Government to meet the requirements of the

February 16, 1987
Automotive Strategy
Canada-U.S. Auto Pact when it comes to assembly and Canadian content.
This means that a car produced in one of the new Japanese plants in Canada will be made or assembled primarily from parts imported from offshore, and therefore will not have the same job-creating potential as the same kind of car assembled in a plant built and operated by one of the Big Four.
A pillar of the strategy which the Canadian Government needs for its auto industry is that all those who wish to sell cars in Canada, above perhaps a certain very minimum level, must play by the same rules, whether they are the Big Four North American producers, the Japanese producers, or the Korean producers. They must meet the same requirements in respect of assembly in Canada and of Canadian content. This means basically the rules under which the big four North American producers operate the Canada-U.S. Auto Pact. Those are simple requirements, straightforward requirements and proven requirements, but so far only one of these new Japanese investors is subject to a clear binding commitment to meet those Auto Pact rules, and that is in the General Motors- Suzuki joint venture because of the commitments extracted from Suzuki by the Ontario Government.
This House should agree that our Government insist by force of law that the Japanese and Korean manufacturers, which are building automotive assembly plants here, meet, within a very short and reasonable deadline, the Auto Pact commitments regarding Canadian content and production ratios. If that does not happen, then surely they cannot be allowed to operate in the same way as the North American producers.
We need to have an automotive strategy in Canada. It must have two pillars. First, the preservation of the Auto Pact and its safeguards; second, to all those who wish to sell cars in Canada the extending of the requirements presently imposed only on North American producers for assembly and Canadian content. Failure to do that this will put at risk 40,000 jobs, something we cannot afford to do. Equally important, it will put at risk what I have said is a cornerstone of the Canadian economy, and we cannot allow this to happen. We need a strategy. The elements of that strategy are clear. We must insist that our Government get on with it, put that strategy in place, and make the Japanese and Korean producers play by the same rules as the North American producers in the interests of the workers in the automotive industry but equally in the interests of the entire community, of our country and all those in it.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING AN AUTOMOTIVE STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for this opportunity to take part in a debate on one of Canada's basic industry, the automotive industry.
The Canadian Government has clearly indicated its support for maintaining a strong and competitive automotive industry
in Canada. Indeed, assembly operations and the manufacture of parts and related components rank as the foremost manufacturing sector in Canada, and I am very pleased to represent certain groups, certain regions of the riding of Chambly that are directly involved in manufacturing either parts or related components for the automotive industry. Incidentally, these firms are doing extremely well these days.
In 1985 this sector shipped various products valued at over $42 billion and employed about 129,000 people. According to Canadian steel manufacturers, the North American automotive industry absorbs roughly 35 per cent of their output. The Conservative Government is very much aware of the fact that North American auto plants make a major contribution to Canada's economy and Canadian consumers. The Government is also aware of the fact that the auto makers are becoming part of an ever more international and competitive industry. As a result, unfortunately North American car manufacturers have lost a share of their market to imported products. What is more, new Asiatic manufacturers who open their plants in North America are increasing the pressure on our domestic industry.
However the North American industry is now undergoing major structural changes. Since the industry's evolution has growing international implications, the Government believes that Canada's auto makers must adopt new manufacturing and management techniques if they want to remain competitive on international markets. This is why we tried to give them time to make the transition. Since 1981 we have maintained an export restriction agreement with Japan, and in the May 1985 Budget we announced measures which were to come into force on January 1, 1987 and which were designed to eliminate provisions under which such countries as Korea and Mexico were allowed to export duty free automotive products.
North American companies are adjusting under this pressure, yet they continue to make huge investments to improve quality and introduce new products while reducing costs. From 1980 to 1985, their capital expenditures in Canada averaged $550 million dollars a year. Let us look for instance at General Motors. We are all aware of the important fact that its Boisbriand plant, in Quebec, is still operating at full capacity. General Motors therefore invested in a number of projects, of which the most important is the $2 billion Auto-plex program for the manufacture of a new line of front wheel drive vehicles. Chrysler and Ford also invested recently in their Canadian plants, mostly to automatize. Because of this, Canada will be in a good position to manufacture highly competitive cars, such as the American Motors Premier, the General Motors GM-I0, and naturally, the Chrysler van which is manufactured in Windsor and already very popular.
As concerns foreign investment, we have tried to guarantee that Canada will have a fair share of Japanese investments in North America which, until quite recently, went for the most part to the United States. Without these investments in Canada, Japanese companies could import vehicles from their
February 16, 1987

new assembly plants in the United States and increase their share of our market without contributing to the Canadian economy.
Since 1982, the Japanese have been spending a lot of money on assembly plants in North America to strengthen their market and minimize the effects of possible trade restrictions. Honda and Toyota plan to invest $600 million to build an assembly plant in Canada. The GM/Suzuki partnership will invest $500 million and Hyundai will spend $300 million for an assembly plant at Bromont, in Quebec. Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege of attending the sod turning ceremony for this Hyundai plant in Bromont. Some 480,000 vehicles will be manufactured in Canada. These investments should create some 5,000 jobs directly, as well as a great number of indirect jobs, especially in the Chambly constituency. If a number of other projects go forward, thousands of additional jobs could be created in Canada.
We recognize that, in the beginning, these plants will use fewer workers and rely more on foreign parts suppliers than their North American competitors. However, we shall try to ensure that these new Canadian companies maximize the Canadian added value of their products and that, by so doing, they get gradually closer to compliance with the Auto Pact. There will be more openings for Canadian parts manufacturers. We know that they will try to determine which products could be supplied to these newcomers and we shall co-operate closely with them in this regard. Until now, certain Japanese and Canadian firms have gone into partnership to manufacture a whole range of products including instrument panels and rubber products. In addition, several Canadian and European companies have co-operated in joint ventures to produce sophisticated parts and accessories.
During our talks with Japanese and Korean car manufacturers, we insisted on the importance of the Auto Pact's goals and performanced requirements. It is important to stress that companies choosing to comply with the Auto Pact derive significant tariff benefits. Although they are under no obligation to comply, financial benefits cannot be ignored in a highly competitive climate. In fact, all new entrants, including Toyota, Honda and Hyundai have announced plans to comply with the Auto Pact.
Up till now, Mr. Speaker, the Government has been applying the general principle of encouraging rather than requiring the establishment of performance levels in Canada. We are not a dictatorial government, Mr. Speaker. Clearly, if we were to enact Canadian content legislation, we would be violating our multilateral trade obligations under the GATT. Not to mention eventual reactions by our trade partners, there is no indication that increased protection would improve the Canadian industry's competitive position or guarantee job creation. In fact, recent productivity and competitivity gains obtained by the Canadian industry largely stem from deep changes companies have been making in manufacturing methods and products, in the face of strong international competition.
Automotive Strategy
Mr. Speaker, we are not convinced that increased restrictions will encourage North American and foreign manufacturers to invest in this country. Rather, the Canadian Government, in co-operation with provinces, will encourage significant automotive investments by creating a stable economic climate and implementing appropriate monetary and fiscal policies.
However, Mr. Speaker, the Government recognizes that the automotive industry is facing new problems that call for novel solutions. In that context, I would like to take this opportunity to inform Hon. Members that the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion has agreed to consult industry and labour representatives on a wide range of matters of importance to the automotive industry.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the Minister recently met representatives of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association, Canadian Automotive Workers and the Society of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers, to examine industry matters, including the one now before the House, and to look for solutions.
It is my belief, Mr. Speaker, that together we can establish policies that will ensure the industry's long-term viability and its contribution to the Canadian economy.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING AN AUTOMOTIVE STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think anyone can sit in this Chamber for very long, regardless from what part of Canada he or she comes, before beginning to realize the importance of the auto industry in the Canadian economy. Before very long, he or she will also come to the realize that the auto industry is in somewhat of a crisis.
The importance of this afternoon's debate is that the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) has suggested some ways to resolve this crisis and has pointed to potential solutions. His motion calls for legislation in the spirit of the Auto Pact, legislation which would apply to all automobile manufacturers who wanted to access the Canadian market. For vehicles that would be sold in the Canadian market, there would be a requirement that the manufacturers would have to reach a basic 60 per cent equivalent of Canadian content.
In the last few years, there has been a great deal of legitimate concern about the flood of Japanese and Korean imports. At present, more than 30 per cent of all automobiles purchased in Canada come from these two countries. It is expected that if current trends continue, this figure will increase to between 35 per cent and 40 per cent in two years. These are good cars. They are reliable and serviceable. The problem is that they do not produce Canadian jobs. In fact, as they replace cars that are made under the Auto Pact, they displace Canadian jobs.
Coming from British Columbia where there is an exceedingly high unemployment rate today, I must admit that I am slightly envious of members from central Canada where the

February 16, 1987
Automotive Strategy
unemployment rate is considerably lower. Certainly the Auto Pact has had a good deal to do with the prosperity central Canada is enjoying right now. The motion we are discussing today, however, opens up the possibility that some of this prosperity could be shared by western Canada. Hon. Members who spoke previously already mentioned the wheel assembly plant Toyota is building in British Columbia, but this is minuscule in comparison to the number of cars sold in British Columbia and in comparison to the number of jobs that exist in the auto industry. We would like to see more jobs in western Canada. As a western Canadian, I do recognize the need of people in central Canada to protect the jobs that already exist.
The Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor pointed out that while we are in a surplus relationship with the United States, our over-all automobile trade is in a deficit position because of imports from Japan, Korea and Europe. Many of these companies have production facilities in Canada, but these facilities do not reach Auto Pact levels. Although some of them plan to reach Auto Pact levels, there have been no guarantees. It is expected that they will grow to only approximately 25 per cent to 30 per cent of Canadian content by the end of the decade rather than the 60 per cent of Canadian content required.
The combination of productive over-capacity with a rather flat demand will lead to ever-increasing competition in automobile sales. The share of the market covered by companies included in the Auto Pact could shrink to as little as 40 per cent by 1990. That means that an estimated 40,000 direct jobs could be lost. If we include the ancillary industries, it could mean that as many as 130,000 jobs in related industries could be lost. This is something Canada cannot afford, whether those jobs are lost in central Canada, western Canada or wherever.
The answer we have often heard from whatever Party is in power is that voluntary restraints are being negotiated. However, voluntary restraints have not been very helpful in the past. Under voluntary restraints, Japan's share of the market has gone from 18 per cent two years ago to 21 per cent today. Hyundai, a company from Korea, under duty-free access which was in effect a $ 100-million tax break, now has 8 per cent of the market in Canada. Imports have grown from a value of $332 million in the first half of 1981 to $2.6 billion in the first half of 1986. This gives us some idea of the rapid increase in the problem with which we are dealing.
We need to remember that the automotive sector is the most important part of Canada's manufacturing industry. There is a basic need to ensure that it is not destroyed. A good deal of Canada's economic health depends upon the extraction of raw resources, and in many ways we have a resource-based economy. However, in western and northern Canada, we are seeing the weakness of that kind of an economy. As resources become depleted, world markets become glutted or certain resources become obsolete, the economy that is dependent on those resources will become weak and have little flexibility.
There is a need for a strong manufacturing sector that will be able to diversify.
The motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Essex- Windsor provides that if companies want to have access to the Canadian maAet, they will have to pay for it. They will need to pay for it by making a commitment to Canadian content. Sixty per cent of the value of everything sold in Canada will have to have the equivalent of 60 per cent Canadian content value added. This is a way to protect jobs we already have. It is a way to ensure that the prosperity we see in central Canada will remain and also to ensure that some of that prosperity will go to other parts of Canada like western Canada where there are very great needs indeed.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING AN AUTOMOTIVE STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will speak for a few minutes and then my colleague, the Hon. Member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart), will conclude. When speaking of the Auto Pact and the auto industry, Hon. Members seem to view it as a static situation. When the Auto Pact was put in place in 1965, Studebaker and Hudson were in the market. In fact, at one stage Renault had a manufacturing plant in Montreal and Toyota had one in Nova Scotia. They are gone and Toyota of course has recently opened a new plant in the Cambridge area.
The perspective I want to bring to this debate is that we are talking about a global industry. General Motors recently made an agreement with Volvo to produce certain models of trucks and buses in a joint venture. The Chevrolet division of GM imports Suzuki trucks from Japan and sells them through its dealer network. General Motors also sells two or three other automobile models by way of joint venture or direct import from Japan. Everyone is very familiar with the recent deal they made with Suzuki to produce that vehicle in southwestern Ontario. From their perspective it is a global industry. Ford Motor Company recently announced a joint venture with Volkswagen in Brazil. I do not know whether some of that production will come to Canada but I understand Volkswagen will run the plant, Ford will sell the production and have some engineering say so. Ford has a model in its line which was designed by Mazda. It is being produced in Taiwan, shipped to Canada and sold under the Ford name. Ford also brings in a sports car from Germany. Ford is a substantial investor in Mazda, which the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) will be pleased to know.
Chrysler Corporation has an array of automobiles which are either imported from Japan or have Japanese components. American Motors is controlled by Renault. Renault owns Mack trucks, which a lot of people do not realize. White Motor Company is controlled by Volvo. Freightliner is owned by Mercedes Benz. Discussions are under way between a Japanese truck manufacturer and some of the few North American truck manufacturers still in business.
All of these deals have come about for a variety of reasons. Some have to do with development, some with production, and
February 16, 1987

some with service facilities in some parts of the market. Others have to do with common components. By way of example, some European manufacturers are using a common engine block and machining it to their own requirements in order to achieve economies of scale in the casting of engine blocks. Japan is experimenting with a ceramic engine block. There are manufacturers working closely together to produce a common automatic transmission which can be used in small vehicles.
The Auto Pact, when it was crafted by our two Governments, had a little different form than some people believe. On the American side it is a bilateral agreement, while on the Canadian side it is a multilateral agreement. That is why we were able to bring in four cylinder engines from Germany, along with various other components from Brazil, Mexico and other places, to be used in Canadian production. We put them through our manufacturing process, added Canadian content, and then used them domestically and exported them to the U.S.
In my constituency, Tridon Manufacturing has just signed a licensing agreement with a Japanese company to produce windshield wipers. Degguse makes catalytic converters and has just signed a licensing agreement in Japan and Korea, I believe, to produce the ceramic cores for catalytic converters. So as the industry develops it is becoming more and more global in nature and I would not recommend that at this time we put any restrictions on that evolution.
I will stop at this point and yield the floor to my colleague.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING AN AUTOMOTIVE STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I very much appreciate the opportunity to say a few words at the end of the hour set aside for this debate. It is clear that I rise to support the motion of my colleague from Essex- Windsor. I come from a community where half the jobs are related to the automobile industry. There are four plants in my riding and it is natural that I should rise to support a motion in defence of the jobs which are so important in my constituency. However, we should not overlook the fact that the automobile industry is largely responsible, far more than the Government, for the degree of economic improvement we have experienced in the last couple of years. While 50 per cent of the employment in my community depends upon the automotive industry, some 130,000 jobs in total depend directly on it, and indirectly some 430,000 jobs across Canada are dependent upon it. It is perfectly clear that Canadians generally benefit from jobs in the automobile industry which, as was shown earlier, is largely attributable to the effects of the Auto Pact signed some 20 years ago.
I was also pleased to hear the intervention of my colleague from British Columbia who recognized that this motion is of benefit to Canadians generally as well as to his own province. If these measures are adopted then not only Ontario and central Canada will benefit, so will the rest of Canada.
Some have called attention to the fact that there was a time when the importation of Japanese cars meant the availability of a high quality, innovative and attractive product at low prices in comparison with the American product. One of the reasons that we have benefited is that in the last couple of years the North American producers who are signatories to the Auto Pact have improved their technology and product to the stage of being of equal quality to Japanese cars. Most important, the manufacturers of those automobiles in this country produce a lot of jobs. They produce three to four times more jobs than the assembly plants now being established here by offshore producers.

February 16, 1987
Adjournment Debate
The time has come, not to give North American manufacturers any advantage, but to ensure that they will be operating on a level playing field. The Japanese manufacturers, which are establishing assembly-only plants in North America, must be required to play by the same rules. If that is done, Canadian consumers will have good products, whether produced by the big four or the Japanese manufacturers, and Canadian jobs will be maintained. I understand it to be my responsibility and the responsibility of Parliament to act in the interests of the Canadian people.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION-MINISTER'S BROADCAST STATEMENTS. (B) CONTENT OF STATEMENTS
IMMIGRATION-MINISTER'S BROADCAST STATEMENTS. (B) CONTENT OF STATEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a little more this evening about a very unfortunate matter which occurred in January and which questions in the House have not resolved. On January 23 The Montreal Gazette published an article quoting a paragraph from a speech given by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) a few days earlier. The speech included the following paragraph:
A lot of pride, a lot of pride.
That is in reference to his home area. It continues:
Because it's-a protected francophone enclave. Three hundred thousand- undisturbed by immigration, by the presence by other realities in the country. So it has a purity at the demographic level, at the ethno-cultural level, at the ethnocultural level especially.
That paragraph aroused enormous reaction in various quarters in this country, to which I can testify. I know that the Canadian Ethnocultural Council has protested this to the Prime Minister's Office and has urged the withdrawal of these words and an apology to those who make up the other realities in the country to which the Minister referred in this political statement.
The intensely regrettable fact is that this was pressed upon the Minister himself. I can say that advisedly. It was pressed upon him to withdraw the statement and recognize how contentious and objectionable it was to many Canadians. That has not been done. For that reason I felt compelled again, after having raised the matter on January 29, to press the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), in the absence of the
Minister, to have him withdraw this statement in order to have this expunged from the record. That has not been done.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration should be conscious of the words that he uses, what they evoke, and what the dangers are. I want to address that briefly in underscoring the urgency of such a withdrawal. In the process, I want to demonstrate that this is a shallow view, even of the Minister's own region and of the people of whom he is justly proud.
To talk of a protected francophone enclave is to take a very limited view of the Lac St. Jean-Saguenay region. This is, after all, a region in which British and Anglo Canadian trading interests and forestry interests long had a very, very large role. There was a day when William Price was regarded as the uncrowned king of the Saguenay. With that kind of a reality, surely there are realities to consider in asserting that this is a protected francophone enclave. To talk about it as undisturbed or untouched by immigration involves the question of how to translate deranger.
Surely to speak of it in those terms is to ignore what is true for Canadians generally, that we are first a nation which has grown from immigration. The Minister of Employment and Immigration failed to recognize that fact in talking about an area "untouched by", suggesting that here was a native element, a protected francophone enclave, which was not touched by these other realities. That is exactly what has aroused the fear of so many Canadians as to what the Minister actually meant.
To speak about "pure in population and in culture", if I could paraphrase slightly what the Minister actually said, is most assuredly to talk in terms of race. The intensely regrettable thing is that the Minister had pointed out to him that this was precisely the language which in the Third Reich in Germany was the language of Nazi race legislation to be applied to population as a basis for extermination of the Jews and others.
We do not talk about being pure in population and culture. We want to celebrate the richness of culture. As a sort of concluding note on this plea to the Government and to the Minister himself, I note the fact that the Minister responsible for Multiculturalism in the very week this came up in the House was launching an advertising campaign in which he wanted Canadians to realize that Canada is no longer a nation of two solitudes and the others, but rather a family of all of us. There is the most grievous failing of the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
Surely a precise description of one of the solitudes is a protected francophone enclave undisturbed by other realities. It is in the most parochial terms, the worst terms of regional penny politics, to talk about one's home region in that way, especially when one is the Minister responsible for Immigration, instead of celebrating the diversity of the country and enjoying the fact, that "francophonia", if I can use that kind of
February 16, 1987

new word for French-speaking Canadians, has been enriched by immigration to this country. In fact, the City of Montreal and the Province of Quebec have had French-speaking elements added to their population and this has enriched society. To ignore that, even if it is in the Lac-Saint Jean- Saguenay region, was an incredible oversight from our Honourable Minister of Employment and Immigration.

Mr. Speaker, I regret the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) has chosen such a distasteful approach to such a sensitive matter. I regret that he seems to place the partisan business of trying to score political points above any careful consideration of the matter.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration has already made it perfectly clear to all Hon. Members of the House that the characterization given to his words was not only completely contrary to his intention, but completely contrary to his meaning. What is most important here is that such a characterization of his words is also completely contrary to the Minister's demonstrated beliefs, which all of us on this side of the House know. The Minister's meaning was not misunderstood by any who know him or his work. The Minister also said:

Because of a wrong choice of words, this may and does happen. If I thereby insulted anyone, I am deeply sorry.

That was clearly understood. The sincerity and convictions of the Minister are beyond question. All of his actions as a Minister of the Crown gives solid support to his words, which I quote from Hansard of January 29 at page 2879:
-I have the highest regard and respect for all immigrants and refugees who have at last reached a country where they can enjoy freedom.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-(A) LANGUAGE POLICY. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ASSERT ITS POSITION

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-(A) LANGUAGE POLICY. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ASSERT ITS POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this adjournment debate, I would like to pursue with the House the issue of equitable representation within the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the manner in which the Official Languages Act is implemented within a national agency that also has a responsibility to reflect the regional interests of this country.
Mr. Speaker, the House will recall that on December 18, I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) when the Government intended to take a firm and public stand on equitable representation, and to quote the wording of my question: "The Government has adopted a passive attitude in this matter, preferring to do nothing. Delighted with this lack
Adjournment Debate
of action and leadership, the RCMP is still bent on its decision to reduce from 20 to 14 per cent the proportion of francophones among its regular officers."
Mr. Speaker, in the fall of 1986, in a monthly publication called the Pony Express, RCMP Headquarters announced its decision to reduce from 20 to 14 per cent the proportion of francophones among its regular officers. Mr. Speaker, this 20 per cent figure is not something I dreamed up. In fact, it was set in 1982 by the RCMP and Treasury Board in accordance with the requirements of the Official Languages Act, as a target for 1996. It was a policy agreed on by Treasury Board and the RCMP.
In the fall 1986 issue of Pony Express, we read that this figure would be reduced to 14 per cent, and according to documents we received, this was done with the approval of Treasury Board. When I asked my question, the House will recall that the Minister replied: No, certainly not. There will be no relaxing of the implementation of the Official Languages Act, and these agreements are only preliminary agreements, discussions among officials. There have been no concrete decisions, and no decision will be made without our being involved.
I waited, and the fact is that the Committee on Official Languages to which many Members of this House belong asked the RCMP to appear before the committee, and we had an opportunity to question Commissioner Simmonds of this national police force. It turned out to be a rather tumultuous confrontation, as Hon. Members may recall. It all began with the tabling of a unilingual English document, and one might say the situation was somewhat tense because we had the impressison that it might have been a way to humour us or to challenge us. But I think the commissioner just made a mistake and, finally, the meeting got under way, although the proceedings were not fully productive because the answers were not forthcoming. We could not get the commissioner to say whether or not the RCMP was intent on reducing staff from 20 to 14 per cent, which would create difficulties with respect to fair representation on this police force. It would also eliminate forever the possibility of having a sufficient number of employees and officers which would give Canadians an opportunity not only to work but also to be served in their own language whenever they may have dealings with this police force, the RCMP.
Well, the meeting was not an unqualified success, as we recall. Rumour has it that certain members and the Minister himself was heard to say in public after the meeting that he was getting impatient and wanted the problem to be settled. So I asked him a question here in the House on December 18: What is going to happen, when can we expect to have results, and can you give us dates, some kind of time-frame? The Minister replied the following, as shown on page 2263 of Hansard for December 18, 1986:
I wrote my colleague the Solicitor General on October 22 to ask him to submit to Treasury Board at his earliest convenience the plan which the RCMP meant to follow to implement the Treasury Board guidelines. I was told that it would take a few weeks, and I can accept that.

February 16, 1987
Adjournment Debate
This was four months ago, Mr. Speaker. When I raised this issue recently in the House, I was told to be patient and that the report was forcoming. We are still waiting for this famous report and we are really impatient to see what will come out of this.
Early in January, an internal note of the RCMP written by Commander J.E. Julien, of Division C in Quebec, to Commissioner Simmonds related certain points and commented on this established policy to reduce francophone participation from 20 to 14 per cent. In this document, Commander Julien wrote, and I quote, that the RCMP was violating the rights of francophones and that francophone officers felt rejected by the anglophone majority. In other words, Mr. Speaker, this document confirmed everything that we already knew, namely that the RCMP was very reluctant to keep its commitments under the Official Languages Act.
We did not have long to wait for all this to be confirmed. The management of the RCMP appeared before the committee and confirmed in reply to my questions to the commissioner that its established policy was still to reduce its francophone personnel from 20 to 14 per cent and even to 12 per cent and that it had no intention of changing the existing training program, in other words, that nothing would change and that, if it did, the change would be to reduce further its commitment under the law.
Mr. Speaker, we advised the Government of the problem last September. Nothing was done. We restated our concerns and expressed our fears publicly, but still nothing was done. Meanwhile, virtually irreversible policies are being developed and we urgently ask the Government to publish as soon as possible the report of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) which will give us the components of this policy so that we may put an end to this controversy and know exactly where this Government is going after two Throne speeches in which we were promised that something would be done in relation with our official languages. We were told that two years ago and nothing has happened yet. I am asking this Government to act, to do something positive and to publish this long-awaited report.

speakeroldname: Mr. Frangois Gerin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-(A) LANGUAGE POLICY. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ASSERT ITS POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I must say that we have no lesson to learn from the Liberals as far as the use of French is concerned. One good example is the use of French in the House of Commons. Under the Liberal Government, in 1983 and 1984, only 8 percent of our proceedings took place in French. Under our Government it has gone up to 20 percent, a meaningful improvement which is not due to the Liberals. That is the result of unrelenting efforts by our Government in this regard.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), I would like to clarify tonight the matter raised by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). First of all, as the President of the Treasury Board
already said, the language policy applying to federal institutions is set by the Government and in particular by Ministers of the Treasury Board. One of the purposes of the federal language policy is to ensure the full participation of members of both the French and English speaking communities in federal agencies.
Pursuant to the measures approved by the Treasury Board in order to reach that objective, the affected departments and agencies submit to the Treasury Board annual reports on the progress of implementation of the Official Language policy within their organizations. When the participation rate of one or the other language group departs too much from the percentage of that group in the workforce or the general population, the departments or agencies must state how they intend to reach a more acceptable balance in order to conform to their terms of reference as far as language is concerned.
Mr. Speaker, since language is not a discrimination factor under the Human Rights Act, one cannot use the provisions of Section 15 of that Act, such as the Affirmative Action Program, in order to restore a better balance. In that case, staffing procedures followed by departments must be in line with the Public Service Employment Act and the merit principle must be the determining factor in staffing decisions.
One of the measures Treasury Board would consider acceptable would be for instance for a Department to determine a long term quantitative participation objective. Yet, a set of goals or numerical quotas indicating the number of francophones or anglophones to be appointed to a number of positions over a specific period of time would be considered unacceptable. Likewise, members of an official linguistic group could not be promoted by a department or an organization by means of arbitrary identification of the linguistic requirements of the positions or by imperative staffing methods in order to achieve their long term participation objectives.
Finally, concerning the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, as already mentioned by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), Treasury Board has neither considered nor approved any reduction in the participation objectives of regular officers who have indicated French as their first official language. In this connection, the Treasury Board President has asked his colleague the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) for changes which the RCMP would like to make to its plans regarding the implementation of the official language policy and more specifically concerning Francophone participation. That was in December last.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I indicate that the President of Treasury Board wants to assure the House that the Government is aware of the need to readjust the participation of minority official linguistic communities in certain departments where there are shortcomings. This aspect, like others, is currently under consideration in the framework of the comprehensive review of official language policies. Thank you for granting me extra time, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-LEVEL OF BENEFITS. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT CATEGORICALLY REJECT ALL BENEFIT REDUCTIONS
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-LEVEL OF BENEFITS. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT CATEGORICALLY REJECT ALL BENEFIT REDUCTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 3, I raised an extremely important question regarding the recommendations in the report of the Forget Commission, particularly the fact that women especially would be disadvantaged by the implementation of those recommendations. I asked for an undertaking from the Government that neither Canadian women nor men would be disadvantaged in the implementation of any of the recommendations of the Forget Commission.
The main way in which people will be disadvantaged if the recommendations are acted upon is by the ending of the so-called regional extended benefits part of the program and the replacement of the benefit calculations by the use of the so-called annualization principle for calculating benefits.
The idea is to establish eligibility for unemployment insurance after 10 weeks of work, but the earnings for the payment of UI would be based upon earnings over 52 weeks. Of course that would be very disadvantageous for people in areas of high unemployment, especially Atlantic Canada.
The total savings to the unemployment insurance scheme if these recommendations are acted upon are in the order of $3 billion, or about the amount of money spent for regionally extended benefits and for fishermen's special benefits. Of course this money comes from consolidated revenues, from taxpayers' dollars, not from employer-employee contributions.
Specifically there would be losses of $1 billion to Quebec, $540 million to Ontario, $660 million to Atlantic Canada, and $600 million to the west. All parts of the country would certainly be adversely affected.
Let us look at how people would be hurt if there is action on the recommendations. Benefits would go to 66.6 per cent of the last year's earnings or maximum insurable earnings. Therefore, a person who had worked the entire year before would be fairly well off on unemployment insurance. However, for someone who was unemployed for most of the previous year and only worked 10 weeks, the unemployment insurance benefit would provide only 13 per cent of income replacement. That is very little money. For the worker earning $400 per week with 52 weeks worked in the past year, the UI would be $277 per week. An employee in an area of high unemployment with only 10 weeks of work would only be receiving $52 per week. We are not talking about much income replacement. We are talking more about a welfare scheme in terms of its actual impact. Over 75 per cent of UI claimants have worked fewer than 52 weeks before filing a claim. They are the ones who will be hurt, and there are many such people.
Annualization, even with the 66.6 per cent benefit rate, would actually mean that half of Canada's unemployed would
Adjournment Debate
have less than 40 per cent of their week's income replaced by unemployment insurance. These changes mean a starve-out policy for depressed regions and a starve-out welfare program for workers with the least access to new jobs.
Another area of real concern is that women would be hit under annualization. Ironically, while women are supposed to be brought into the system increasingly by including part-time workers, most part-time workers are also seasonal workers. They would be hit as well. The National Action Committee, which wants to speak to the proposals, has been denied access to the committee. It will not have a chance to raise these extremely important issues, and I would hope that would be reconsidered.

We want to see changes which would improve the unemployment insurance scheme and extend its coverage to many more Canadian men and women workers. The NPD wants the inclusion of more workers, especially in areas of culture including the theatre, dancing and music. Artists' associations have been asking for a long time for the inclusion of their members into the unemployment insurance scheme.
The Standing Committee on Communications and Culture has proposed amendments to the tax legislation which would indirectly promote this objective. Unfortunately, neither the Forget Commission nor the Government has directly addressed these concerns, namely, the implementation of measures to give a greater number of Canadians unemployment insurance coverage. In fact, the answer is no. It is not an overly generous system. The measures provided by the vast majority of western industrialized countries are better. The priorities of the NDP are clear and they have been for a long time, since the Party's inception.
In our view, job creation is preferable. Canadians would rather work than collect unemployment insurance. However, an unemployment insurance scheme is absolutely necessary in the present situation. Nevertheless, Canadian men and women have had to wait a long time, for decades, because of resistance on the part of the Conservatives and the Liberals, who have refused to enact such a scheme.
The unemployment insurance scheme is relatively recent, having been established in the forties, and it has been under persistent attack by the private sector since the beginning.

At the very least the Government ought to respond to the concerns I have raised to ensure that any changes to unemployment insurance are to improve the system, not to cut benefits to workers who still need that unemployment system.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), I would like to elaborate further on the question asked by the Hon.

February 16, 1987
Adjournment Debate
Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) on December 3, 1986.
As the Minister indicated, the Government has stated in this House that the purpose of any UI reform would not be to save money on the backs of Canadians. Rather, any reform to the UI program would have as its objective to make the system better. In this regard, it is both reasonable and responsible to consider carefully all recent studies that have reviewed the UI program, such as the Macdonald Royal Commission, the House Commission in Newfoundland and the Commission of Inquiry on Unemployment Insurance.
It is evident from the reactions to these reports that unemployment insurance is important to all Canadians. However, the recommendations of these several studies are not compatible in many instances. In fact, the Commission of
Inquiry was not able to arrive at a consensus. For all of these reasons the Government considers it premature at this stage to give assurances on any specific part of the report. I repeat that the Government will be reviewing UI with the objective of improving it, simplifying it and making it fairer. In this regard, the Government is committed to return to the House by May 15 with its plan to modify and improve on unemployment insurance.
